sets.title: The Weighbridge
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an extract from an original short story set in the Western Australian wheatbelt. The town is fictional.
sets.body:
Every December my father drove the harvest to the bins at Wilgarup, and every December he took one of us with him for the weighing. That year it was my turn, though I was eleven and had begun, privately, to find him boring.

We left before the heat. The truck smelled of diesel and old oranges, and the wheat in the back hissed whenever we took a corner, as if the load were muttering about the road. My father drove with one wrist hooked over the wheel. He did not talk on these trips. He listened to the engine the way other men listened to the cricket, leaning slightly towards it, frowning at things I could not hear.

The queue at the bins was a mile of trucks, all of them painted the same tired colour by dust. Men stood beside their cabs in a loose line of hats and talked about rain that had not come and prices that had not gone up. My father nodded at them. Nobody said much. It was understood, I think, that whatever you had in the back of your truck was the whole of your year, and you did not discuss the whole of your year with a man who might have done better.

When it was our turn he eased the front wheels onto the weighbridge so gently that I felt the truck hesitate, the way a horse hesitates at water. Inside the little office a woman with reading glasses on a chain looked at a dial I could not see. Then she wrote a number on a docket and passed it through the window.

My father read it once. He folded the docket in half, and then in half again, until it was a small hard square, and he put it in the pocket of his shirt, over his heart, and buttoned the pocket.

'Good?' I said.

'It's a number,' he said.

On the way home he stopped at the roadhouse and bought me a lemonade and himself nothing. He sat on the bonnet in the heat with his hat tipped forward, looking at the paddocks we had passed that morning, which now looked exactly the same, stubble to the horizon, a few crows working the edges. I understood that he was doing a sum in his head and that I was not part of it.

It was years before I learned what that number meant: that it had been the worst harvest in a decade, that the bank had already written twice, that my mother had been up at night with the books spread over the kitchen table like a hand of cards that would not come right. Nobody told me. They protected me from it the way you protect a child from weather, by not mentioning it, by buying lemonade.

What I remember now is not the dial, which I never saw, or the number, which I never knew, but the way he buttoned the pocket. As if the year could be kept in there. As if folding a thing small enough made it possible to carry.

questions.model: The farmers come across as a community held together by the same hardship, but one with strict, unspoken rules about pride and privacy. The writer first strips away their individuality. The trucks are "all of them painted the same tired colour by dust", a transferred epithet that hands the men's exhaustion to their vehicles, as if the drought has worn everyone down to the same shade. The men themselves shrink to "a loose line of hats". The synecdoche shows us the badge of their work but never their faces, or whatever is written on them. Even their talk is shaped by absence: "rain that had not come and prices that had not gone up". They circle loss without anyone admitting to his own. The adult narrator then spells out the rule underneath: "whatever you had in the back of your truck was the whole of your year". When "the whole of your year" is repeated in the next clause, its weight lands. Each load is a private verdict on twelve months of work, and comparing loads could shame a man. So they stand together, but guarded, sharing a hardship they have agreed not to discuss.

questions.model:
To a large extent the passage treats silence as a way of caring for the child. Looking back, though, the adult narrator also sees its cost: the silence that sheltered the child also shut them out, and left the father carrying the year alone.

The strongest case for silence as care is the simile that the family protected the narrator "the way you protect a child from weather, by not mentioning it, by buying lemonade." Nobody controls the weather, so the comparison turns the failed harvest into something the parents simply absorb on the child's behalf. The lemonade matters because it stands in for an explanation: something small and sweet is offered instead of the truth. The father's reply, "It's a number," does the same job. Three flat monosyllables are enough to stop the docket's meaning from ever reaching his child.

The passage doesn't let that tenderness go unexamined, however. On the bonnet the father is "doing a sum in his head", and the narrator realises "that I was not part of it." That plain final clause records exclusion, not comfort. The silence is also bigger than one family. At the bins the men talk about "rain that had not come and prices that had not gone up", a ritual of not saying things, policed by the rule that "you did not discuss the whole of your year" with a man who might have done better. Here silence protects pride as much as people, which hints that the father's reticence is partly learned stoicism and not only love.

The ending holds both readings at once. The narrator remembers "the way he buttoned the pocket", and the repeated "As if" fragments expose the hope behind the gesture: that "folding a thing small enough made it possible to carry." The conditional admits the hope was false. The debt didn't shrink; he just carried it where no one could see it. So the passage does present silence as care, but as a care that isolates the person giving it, and the narrator's belated understanding becomes a quiet way of returning it by finally naming what was never said.

sets.title: Sonnet for the Night Bus
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original poem. It is a Petrarchan sonnet: an eight-line octave followed by a six-line sestet.
sets.body:
The last bus out of Central keeps its time
for no one. Every window holds a screen,
a face lit blue above it: nurse in green,
two boys asleep in uniform, the grime
of somebody's whole shift along the line
of someone's sleeve. We do not speak. We lean
the way the bus leans, gently, as if we'd been
rehearsing this together all our lives.

Then, at the bridge, the harbour opens wide—
the whole black water stitched with lights—and one
by one we lift our heads, as if we'd heard
our names called out across it. No one tried
to say what we had seen. The bus moved on.
But for a moment we were all one word.

questions.model: In the octave the passengers are cut off from one another and yet moving as one. Technology seals each of them in: "Every window holds a screen, / a face lit blue above it", so we see a row of separate glowing units rather than a crowd, and the blunt sentence "We do not speak" confirms the silence. But the poet quietly works against that isolation through movement. In "We lean / the way the bus leans, gently", the line break makes the reader tip forward with the passengers, and the collective "we" suggests a unity nobody has chosen or said aloud. The comparison "as if we'd been / rehearsing this together all our lives" turns the sway of the bus into something like choreography. They never speak, but they share a rhythm, and that is their connection.

questions.model: The last line suggests that, for a moment, the harbour turns a busload of strangers into a single meaning. The metaphor "we were all one word" is surprising because the poem has insisted on silence: "We do not speak", and later "No one tried / to say what we had seen." That is the irony. They become "one word" exactly when nobody says anything, so their unity comes from seeing the same thing, not from talking about it. The sestet sets this up when "one / by one we lift our heads, as if we'd heard / our names called out across it." Splitting "one / by one" across the line lets attention spread slowly from person to person, and hearing "our names" suggests each passenger is recognised individually before they merge. Still, the line opens with "But", limits itself to "for a moment", and comes straight after the flat sentence "The bus moved on." The poem celebrates the connection while admitting it doesn't last, leaving the reader with a moment of transcendence that is real but over almost as soon as it begins.

questions.model:
The sonnet form suits this poem extremely well. Its compression, its turn and its rhyme all mirror what the poem is about: a connection that is ordered, intense and brief.

The Petrarchan structure splits the experience in two. The octave is closed in and inward-looking, with "a face lit blue" and "the grime / of somebody's whole shift" keeping each passenger inside a tired, private world. Then the volta arrives at line 9, "Then, at the bridge, the harbour opens wide", and the poem opens up exactly as the view does. The traditional turn of thought becomes a literal turn of the head, so the convention is being used, not just followed.

The rhyme is working too. Several pairs are slant rather than full, like "time" and "lives" or "one" and "on", so the sounds almost match but not quite, like strangers who share a space without really meeting. The final pair, "heard" and "word", is a full rhyme, and it falls on the moment of unity, which makes the closure feel complete.

The form's brevity may be its best feature. Fourteen lines leave no room to explain the connection or stretch it out, and the poem doesn't try: "The bus moved on." Those plain monosyllables put us back in motion, which makes "for a moment" in the last line feel earned rather than sentimental. Free verse might have lingered on the harbour. The sonnet frames the experience as tightly as memory does, so the form doesn't just hold the moment; it acts out how quickly it passes.

sets.title: What the Map Leaves Out
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original speech. The speaker, Dr Rania Saab, a paramedic, is fictional. She is addressing the graduating Year 12 students at the western Sydney high school she once attended.
sets.body:
Thank you, Mr Nguyen. Thank you, parents, grandparents, and the little brother in the third row who has clearly been promised something if he sits still.

Twenty years ago I sat where you are sitting, in a polyester gown that smelled of the storeroom, and I listened to a man in a very good suit tell us that the world was our oyster. I remember thinking two things. The first was that I had never eaten an oyster. The second was that if the world was an oyster, someone had already been told where the pearls were, and it was not us.

I am not here to tell you the world is your oyster. I am here to tell you about maps.

In my first year on the road as a paramedic, I was sent to a call in a street I had driven past a hundred times. The address was on the screen. The map was on the screen. The map said turn left. The map did not say that the left turn had been closed for roadworks for three weeks, or that the house numbers jumped from 14 to 40 because of a subdivision nobody had bothered to tell the council about, or that the woman we were looking for would be on the footpath in her dressing-gown, waving a tea towel so we could find her.

We found her because a boy on a bike, maybe ten years old, pedalled in front of the ambulance shouting, 'This way! This way!' He knew the street. He knew it because he lived in it. No satellite has ever known a street the way a ten-year-old on a bike knows it.

I have thought about that boy for twenty years.

Here is what he taught me. A map is a promise made by people who have never been where you are going. It is useful. Use it. But do not mistake it for the place. Some of you have been handed maps already: by your marks, by your postcode, by what people expect of a kid from here. Some of those maps will say turn left. Some of them will say there is nothing down this road worth seeing. Some of them will say, kindly, in a very good suit, that the pearls are elsewhere.

They are wrong about this suburb. I know because I have driven every street of it at three in the morning with the sirens off, and I have been let into kitchens where grandmothers who spoke no English made me eat before I could leave. I have seen teenagers do CPR on their fathers because a teacher in this hall made them practise on a dummy in Year 9. I have seen people who were told they would amount to nothing hold this place together with their bare hands.

So do not wait for someone to tell you where the pearls are. Be the boy on the bike. Know your street. Know it so well that when the map fails, and it will fail, you are the one who can say: this way.

And when you have learned your way, come back and shout it to the next ambulance, the next new teacher, the next frightened kid in a polyester gown.

This way. This way. Congratulations, and thank you.

questions.model:
The map stands for the expectations other people place on the young, and the speaker uses it to show her audience that those expectations can be wrong, and that knowing a place from the inside can be worth more.

She starts with a story rather than an idea. "The address was on the screen. The map was on the screen. The map said turn left" has the flat, repetitive rhythm of a machine that is sure of itself, and the next sentences knock that confidence down, repeating "The map did not say" before a long list of everything the technology missed. By the end of the list, official knowledge looks thin next to real streets.

The boy on the bike is the alternative. His shout of "This way! This way!" gives local knowledge a voice, and the claim that "No satellite has ever known a street the way a ten-year-old on a bike knows it" puts a child above the most powerful, distant technology there is.

Only after the story does she define her terms: "A map is a promise made by people who have never been where you are going." She is fair to maps ("It is useful. Use it"), but the warning "do not mistake it for the place" points straight at the graduates. The tricolon of maps handed out "by your marks, by your postcode, by what people expect of a kid from here" names the judgements these particular students face, widening from the personal to the social.

By the end, "Be the boy on the bike" has turned the metaphor into an instruction. The audience has moved from people who follow maps to people who can correct them.

questions.model:
The structure works because it is circular and builds as it goes. She opens with a borrowed cliché, swaps it for a story the audience can own, and finishes by handing that story back to them as a job to do.

The opening uses humour to win over a ceremonial crowd. Thanking "the little brother in the third row" nods to the families and loosens the formality, and her memory of "a man in a very good suit" announcing that "the world was our oyster" sets up the cliché she is about to take apart. Her two private thoughts, that she "had never eaten an oyster" and that "someone had already been told where the pearls were", turn the joke into a sharp point about privilege. Then the short sentence "I am here to tell you about maps" changes direction and signals a more honest frame.

The middle moves from story to lesson to application. Telling the paramedic story before stating any message is persuasive, because the audience feels the map fail before anyone explains what that means. The one-line paragraph "I have thought about that boy for twenty years" gives the story weight and slows the pace for reflection.

What gives the structure its power is the return to the opening images. The cliché comes back when maps "will say, kindly, in a very good suit, that the pearls are elsewhere", and she answers bluntly: "They are wrong about this suburb." Her evidence is local and emotional: grandmothers who "made me eat before I could leave", and teenagers doing CPR because "a teacher in this hall" made them practise. That phrase "this hall" ties abstract hope to the room the audience is sitting in.

The ending closes the circle. The "frightened kid in a polyester gown" is her younger self, and the repeated "This way. This way." turns the boy's words into a shared motto. Finishing on that echo means the audience leaves with their own instructions rather than with her achievements. If there is a weakness, it is that the optimism rests on anecdote rather than wider evidence. For a graduation audience that needs belief more than data, though, the structure is judged exactly right.

sets.title: The Year of the Broken Arm
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original piece of memoir-style writing. The narrator and her family are fictional.
sets.body:
My sister broke her arm in the summer of 1998, and for twenty-five years we have disagreed about whose fault it was.

In my version, which I have told at three weddings and one funeral, we are at our grandparents' place in Mildura, and the fig tree in the backyard is the size of a house. Ellie is nine and I am eleven. She wants to climb to the high fork, where the figs are, because the birds have already got all the low ones. I tell her not to. I say it clearly, in an older-sister voice I have been practising, and then I go inside to watch the cricket with Pop. A minute later there is a sound like a stick snapping under a boot, and then nothing, and then Ellie screaming in a way I had not known a person could scream.

In Ellie's version, I dared her.

She is very calm about this. She says it the way you would say the date. 'You said I was too chicken to get to the fork,' she says. 'You said it twice. And then you went inside because you didn't want to watch me do it.' She says this at Christmas, over the pavlova, and my mother looks at the ceiling, and my partner looks at me with the interest of someone watching a documentary.

The difficulty is that I can see her version. I can see it quite clearly, which is the problem. I can see myself at the foot of the tree with my arms folded, and I can hear my voice saying chicken, and I don't know whether this is a memory or whether I have simply heard her story so many times that it has grown its own pictures, the way a room you have only heard described begins, after a while, to have furniture.

Memory, I have read, is not a recording but a performance. Each time we remember something we rebuild it from parts, and each time the parts are slightly different, like a cover band that has played the same song so often it has forgotten the original. This is meant to be comforting. It is not comforting. It means that somewhere in my head there is an eleven-year-old who either told her sister to be careful or told her to be brave, and I cannot get her to tell me which.

What neither of us disputes is the hospital. The fluorescent light, the plaster going on white and warm, the nurse who let Ellie choose the colour of the cast, and the way she chose purple, then looked at me, and said I could be the first to sign it. I wrote my name so small that it disappeared under everyone else's by the end of the week.

I have been thinking about why I did that. It is possible I was being modest. It is possible I was ashamed. It is possible that even then, at eleven, I was already beginning to revise.

The writer never delivers a verdict, but she steers the reader so that Ellie's version slowly becomes the more believable one, and the narrator's honesty about that becomes the real subject of the passage.

The narrator's own version arrives with confident, almost cinematic detail: the fig tree "the size of a house" and the exact sound, "like a stick snapping under a boot". Then she undercuts herself by admitting she has told the story "at three weddings and one funeral". That sounds like a polished routine, not a raw memory.

Ellie's version earns its credibility through tone and precision. She is "very calm about this" and says it "the way you would say the date", a simile that makes her claim sound like plain fact. She remembers the exact taunt and adds "You said it twice", and the motive she gives her sister, that she "didn't want to watch", is uncomfortably believable.

The biggest shift comes when the narrator concedes, "I can see her version." Her comparison to a described room that begins "to have furniture" shows how retelling can manufacture pictures. That weakens both versions, but hers more, since it is her memory being reshaped. The image of memory as "a cover band" that "has forgotten the original" widens the problem, so we stop thinking about lying and start thinking about how unstable ordinary memory is.

It's subtle and effective steering. By ending on the tiny signature and the word "revise", the writer lets us suspect the narrator's guilt while admiring her for refusing to defend herself.

sets.title: Unexpected Item in the Bagging Area
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original opinion column written in the style of a regional newspaper. The columnist, Margaret Ellery, and the supermarket are fictional.
sets.body:
The new self-checkouts arrived at our supermarket on a Tuesday, which seems fitting. Nothing good has ever started on a Tuesday.

There are six of them now where Lorraine's register used to be. They are very clean. They speak in the voice of a woman who has never had a bad day in her life, and they want me to know, several times per transaction, that there is an unexpected item in the bagging area.

I want to be fair to the machines. They are fast, mostly. They do not take smoko. They do not, as far as I know, go home to a sick husband and come back the next morning with their lipstick on anyway. The company says they 'free up staff for customer service', and I'm sure somebody in a head office believes that, in the same way I am sure somebody believes the twelve-items-or-fewer sign is a law of nature.

But I have been shopping at that supermarket for thirty-one years, and here is what Lorraine knew that the machine does not. She knew that my mother had died, because she asked after her every Thursday for nine years and then one Thursday I could not answer, and she reached across the conveyor belt and held my wrist for a second, and then she scanned my teabags. She knew that the young bloke from the mechanic's buys the same pie every day and that if he didn't come in, someone should ring the garage. She knew which of the old men only came in to talk.

I don't have a graph to show you. I can't tell you what Lorraine was worth in dollars. That is rather my point. The things that hold a small town together don't show up on the spreadsheet, and so the spreadsheet concludes, quite reasonably, that they do not exist.

Some readers will say I am being sentimental. Fair enough. I am a sixty-four-year-old woman writing a column about a cash register; sentiment is my natural habitat. Others will say that progress is progress, and that people complained about the automatic car wash too. They did. They were right about that as well: there is nobody left at the car wash either.

So here is my modest proposal. Keep the machines, if you must. But keep one lane with a person in it. Call it the slow lane. Put a sign on it: For people who would like to be known. I suspect the queue will surprise you.

In the meantime, I have started going through the self-checkout with a single lemon, every day, just to keep the machine company. It thanks me for shopping with it. I tell it that's all right, love. Neither of us is fooled. But one of us, at least, is trying.

She mocks the self-checkouts' fake cheer by giving them the voice of "a woman who has never had a bad day in her life", which already sets the machine against the human worker whose loss she will mourn. Then she pulls back: "I want to be fair to the machines", and they are "fast, mostly". That concession makes her sound reasonable rather than merely nostalgic. Mixing humour with fairness earns her the trust she will need when she turns to Lorraine.

She starts with the company's claim that the machines "free up staff for customer service", and deflates it by lumping it in with people who believe "the twelve-items-or-fewer sign is a law of nature". The sarcasm makes the claim sound like a handy corporate fiction. Later she names the charge most likely to be thrown at her: "Some readers will say I am being sentimental." questions.model:
For a reader who likes self-checkouts, the column is very persuasive, because it never asks them to give up on efficiency. It uses a disarming persona, one strong anecdote and a modest, practical proposal to shift attention from what machines do well to what they can't measure.

A sceptical reader is likely to be won over first by her fairness. She grants that the machines "are fast, mostly" and "do not take smoko", and her jokes target corporate language, not people who like technology. Because she gives ground early, her criticism later on reads as balanced rather than cranky.

The anecdote about Lorraine is the emotional centre of the column and its best evidence. Lorraine "reached across the conveyor belt and held my wrist for a second, and then she scanned my teabags". The understatement is what makes it work: the return to an ordinary task straight after the gesture of comfort shows care built into routine work. The repeated "She knew" then widens the example from one person's grief to the welfare of a whole community, right down to the warning that "someone should ring the garage". A cashier becomes an informal safety net. A sceptic can wave away nostalgia, but it is much harder to wave away the loss of that kind of attention.

She then turns her lack of data into an argument: "The things that hold a small town together don't show up on the spreadsheet". The irony of the spreadsheet concluding, "quite reasonably", that such things "do not exist" exposes a flaw in the opposing logic without attacking the people who hold it.

Finally, the proposal is small enough to say yes to: "keep one lane with a person in it." The sign "For people who would like to be known" sticks because it names a need most of us share. Buying "a single lemon" to keep the machine company is funny and sad at once, and the last line, "But one of us, at least, is trying", quietly makes the reader part of the choice. Resting so much on one anecdote is a weakness, but the persona and the proposal make the column very hard for even a committed sceptic to brush off.

sets.title: The Interpreter
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an extract from an original short story; Text 2 is an original poem. Both are about language and family across generations.
sets.body:
The doctor talks to me, not to my father. This is the first thing I notice, and I am fourteen, so I notice it with a kind of pleasure.

'Ask him whether the pain is sharp or dull,' she says. 'Ask him how long.'

I turn to my father. He is sitting very straight on the plastic chair, his good jacket buttoned, his hands on his knees the way he sits in the photographs from before. I ask him in Vietnamese, and I make the question gentler on the way through, because the doctor's English is quick and flat and my father's ears go red when people are quick with him.

'Since Tết,' he says. 'It is nothing. Tell her it is nothing.'

'Since about February,' I tell the doctor. 'He says it's sharp sometimes.'

He did not say that. But I have heard him at night, the small sound he makes turning over, and I think the doctor should know. My father watches my mouth while I speak, trying to catch the shape of his own words in it. I watch him watching me. Between us there is a little bridge made of my voice, and I am the only one who can walk across it.

The doctor writes something. She asks about his work, the lifting, the hours. I translate warehouse and night shift and twenty-two years. I do not translate the part where he says, 'Tell her I have never missed a day,' because the doctor has already looked at the clock, and because I know it would sound, in English, like a man asking for a medal.

On the way out the receptionist says something about a referral, and my father nods as if he understands, and thanks her twice in his careful English, and I see her smile at him the way people smile at children who have said a new word. I want to tell her he was an engineer once. I want to tell her he can recite poems I will never be able to read. Instead I take the paper from her and fold it into my school bag.

In the car he says, 'What did you tell her?'

'Everything,' I say.

He starts the engine and does not look at me, and I understand that he knows I am lying, and that he is grateful, and that both of these things are true at once, the way it is both day and night somewhere at every minute.

pair.title: Mother Tongue
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
My grandmother kept her language in a tin
with the buttons and the rubber bands,
and when I was small she would open it for me:
words like boiled sweets, sharp at the edges,
that she placed on my tongue and told me not to swallow.

I swallowed them. I was a child.
I swallowed the word for the blue hour after rain
and the word for the cousin who does not visit
and the word for the ache you get from loving a place
that is not where you are.

Now she is ninety and the tin is empty,
or I have lost the key, or there was never a key,
only her hands, which were the key.
On the phone she says a sentence and waits.
I say, Yes, Nonna. I say, Me too.
I say the three words I still own
as if they were the whole of the house.

Somewhere inside me is a room
where all those swallowed words are still dissolving,
sweetening something I can't name.
I go there sometimes. I don't turn on the light.

She makes the doctor's questions "gentler on the way through" because her father's ears "go red when people are quick with him"; she is alert to every small humiliation. She also adds what he holds back. She tells the doctor the pain is "sharp sometimes", having heard "the small sound he makes turning over" at night, and so overrides his stoic "It is nothing." And she drops his claim that he has "never missed a day", afraid it would sound "like a man asking for a medal". Each decision shows a protective, almost parental care, and the usual roles of father and child are reversed.

questions.model: In Text 2 the loss happens slowly, is partly the speaker's own doing, and ends up living inside her. The language is kept "in a tin / with the buttons and the rubber bands", which makes it domestic and precious but also fragile, a household treasure rather than something public. The words are "like boiled sweets, sharp at the edges", a simile that captures how good they felt, yet the instruction "not to swallow" suggests a language has to be held and used, not consumed. The confession "I swallowed them. I was a child." is blunt, two short sentences that carry guilt and self-forgiveness at once. In the third stanza the speaker cycles through uncertainties: the tin is empty, "or I have lost the key, or there was never a key, / only her hands". She is realising the language lived in her grandmother's presence and can't be recovered without her. Treating the "three words I still own" "as if they were the whole of the house" shows how little is left. Even so, the words are "still dissolving, / sweetening something I can't name". The loss isn't total; the language survives as feeling rather than speech.

questions.model:
In both texts language carries love between generations, and in both it also divides the people it connects. Text 1 places that tension in a public, practical setting where the child holds the linguistic power. Text 2 is private and inward, and the child has given that power away.

In Text 1, language connects through the narrator herself. She is "a little bridge made of my voice", the only link between her father and the doctor, but the bridge isolates her too: "I am the only one who can walk across it." For the father, English is a barrier. His "careful English" earns the kind of smile given to "children who have said a new word", a simile that shows how the language shrinks him to a child. Her unspoken wish to say "he was an engineer once" makes clear that what can't be translated is his dignity.

Text 2 runs the loss the other way. Here the older generation holds the richer language and the younger one has let it slip: "I swallowed them. I was a child." The narrator of Text 1 chooses what to leave out; the speaker of Text 2 has no choices left. On the phone she can only manage "Yes, Nonna" and "Me too", an exchange in which love lasts while meaning thins. The barrier isn't a doctor's clock but time itself, figured in the tin that is now "empty".

Yet both texts suggest connection can outlast words. In Text 1 the father "does not look at me", but the narrator knows he knows she is lying and is "grateful", an understanding caught in her comparison that "it is both day and night somewhere at every minute." In Text 2 the lost words are "still dissolving, / sweetening something I can't name", so language moves from speech into feeling. One through prose narrative and the other through lyric metaphor, the texts suggest that between generations language is never simply a bridge or a wall. It is both, and love often lives in the silence where translation fails.

sets.title: Penalty
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original short scene written for performance. The characters are fictional.
sets.body:
A car parked outside a suburban soccer ground, late afternoon. DANNY (12) sits in the passenger seat in a muddy uniform, boots still on. His father, MARK (40s), is in the driver's seat. The engine is off. A trophy, not theirs, glints through the windscreen as another family walks past.

MARK: Seatbelt.

(DANNY doesn't move. MARK waits, then reaches across and does it up for him, the way he did when DANNY was small. DANNY lets him.)

MARK: You want the radio?

DANNY: No.

MARK: Right.

(Pause. MARK taps the steering wheel, two beats, stops.)

MARK: The keeper guessed right. That's all that was. Fifty-fifty. Professionals miss those.

DANNY: You said go left.

MARK: I said — (He stops.) I said if you're not sure, go left.

DANNY: I was sure. I was going to go right. Then I looked at you.

(Silence. Outside, someone toots a horn and cheers. MARK watches them in the rear-view mirror until they are gone.)

MARK: When I was your age, my dad came to one game. One. Under-thirteens, against Penrith. I scored twice and he left at half-time because the car was making a noise.

DANNY: You've told me.

MARK: Have I.

DANNY: Every time we lose.

(MARK almost laughs. It doesn't quite arrive.)

MARK: So I come to all of them. Every Saturday. I thought that was — I thought if I was there, you'd...

DANNY: I know.

MARK: Do you?

(DANNY looks at his boots. He starts unlacing one, slowly, very carefully, as if it matters.)

DANNY: Next time can you stand somewhere I can't see you?

(It lands. MARK sits with it. He takes his hands off the wheel and puts them in his lap.)

MARK: Yeah. (Beat.) Yeah, mate. I can do that.

DANNY: Not far. Just — behind the goal or something. Where the other dads are.

MARK: Behind the goal.

DANNY: So I know you're there. I just don't want to look.

(MARK nods. He starts the car. The radio comes on by itself, loud, a song neither of them likes. Neither of them turns it off.)

MARK: Maccas?

DANNY: (after a moment) Yeah.

(MARK pulls out. As the car turns, DANNY reaches over and turns the radio down, just a little. MARK lets him. Lights fade.)

The ending settles the immediate conflict through a small compromise on both sides, but it only partly deals with the deeper pattern of pressure handed down from father to son. That is what makes it convincing rather than neat.

The turning point is Danny's request: "Next time can you stand somewhere I can't see you?" The direction "It lands" tells us how hard it hits, and Mark takes "his hands off the wheel" and puts them "in his lap", a gesture of giving up control. "Yeah, mate. I can do that" is plain, but he means it.

Danny's follow-up keeps the emotional balance: "So I know you're there. I just don't want to look." He separates presence from pressure, reassuring Mark that he's wanted while drawing a boundary. That changes how we hear Mark's story about his own absent father. Danny doesn't want the absence Mark suffered, only some distance, so the cycle is adjusted rather than repeated.

The last moments make peace through actions. A loud song "neither of them likes" keeps playing, since "Neither of them turns it off", which suggests a shared, tolerant discomfort, and "Maccas?" / "Yeah." brings back ordinary routine. Most telling of all, Danny turns the radio down "just a little" and "MARK lets him". It mirrors the seatbelt at the start, but reversed: now the son acts and the father allows it.

Not everything is resolved, though. Mark's "Do you?" never gets an answer, and his need to be there hasn't gone away. The ending works because it settles this conflict in a modest, believable way while admitting the two of them will keep negotiating the distance.

sets.title: The Housekeeper, to the New Girl
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original dramatic monologue written in an older style. It is set in a wealthy Sydney household in the 1880s; the speaker is a fictional housekeeper addressing a newly hired maid. A 'character' was a written reference from a former employer; the 'copper' was a large boiler used for washing clothes.
sets.body:
Mind how you set the tray, girl. Silver first,
then china, then yourself, and last of all
your opinions, which in this house are kept
like spoons that are not ours to use. Sit down.
You'll not sit often here, so learn it now.

The mistress rings at seven. Not before.
You'll know her bell; it has a peevish note,
as if the house had wronged it in the night.
The master takes his tea at eight, alone,
and reads the shipping news aloud to no one.
You'll answer when he speaks. He does not speak.

The girl before you? Bridget. Clever hands.
She dressed the mistress's hair as if it mattered,
and sang at the copper, which I let her do,
for there's no rule against a song, God knows,
though there is one against its being heard.
A brooch was lost in March. A garnet brooch.
The mistress turned the house out like a drawer
and found it nowhere, and found Bridget handy.
They sent her off without a character.
You'll know what that means soon enough, I'd wager.

The young master came home that week from town
with a new watch-chain and a careless laugh.
I keep the linen. I keep the household books.
I keep my counsel, which is the hardest keeping.
Don't look at me like that. Pour out the tea.

You'll do. You're quiet. Quiet girls do well.
And if you hear the copper singing, girl,
on wash-days, when the steam is thick and low,
you'll tell yourself it's only water boiling.

Her ordered list, "Silver first, / then china, then yourself", ranks the girl below the objects she polishes, and "last of all / your opinions" puts her inner life at the very bottom. Comparing opinions to "spoons that are not ours to use" implies that a servant's thoughts really belong to her employers: she may keep them, but never use them. Even "Sit down" is immediately undercut by "You'll not sit often here", so rest, like opinion, is a rare privilege. In these brisk commands we hear a woman who has absorbed the hierarchy and now enforces it.

questions.model: Through placement, implication and the speaker's guarded tone, the poet lets us work out that the young master took the brooch, not Bridget, and that the housekeeper knows it. The accusation against Bridget is told sardonically: the mistress "found it nowhere, and found Bridget handy", and the repeated "found" exposes how convenient the scapegoat was. Then, straight after Bridget's dismissal and across the stanza break, comes a detail that seems unrelated: the young master returned "with a new watch-chain and a careless laugh". The speaker never connects the two, but putting them side by side invites us to infer that the garnet brooch paid for the chain, and "careless" suggests he doesn't care who was hurt. In "I keep the linen. I keep the household books." the repetition reminds us she sees the accounts, and so she knows. The climax, "I keep my counsel, which is the hardest keeping", admits what her silence costs her. When she suddenly snaps, "Don't look at me like that", it seems the new girl has understood too, which confirms our inference. The whole accusation is made by implication.

questions.model:
The poem invites a good deal of sympathy for the housekeeper, but not unlimited sympathy. She is complicit in an unjust household, yet the dramatic monologue lets us hear what that complicity costs her, so she comes across as both an agent of the hierarchy and one of its casualties.

The case against her is plain. She trains the new girl to erase herself, ranking "yourself" below silver and china, and she knew Bridget was dismissed "without a character" and did nothing. "You'll know what that means soon enough, I'd wager" has a hint of threat in it, and her closing advice, that the girl should tell herself "it's only water boiling", asks her to adopt the same deliberate blindness. In this sense she keeps the injustice going.

But the poet keeps signalling that her hardness is a way of surviving powerlessness. The mistress's bell has "a peevish note, / as if the house had wronged it", and the master "does not speak"; these are petty, indifferent employers, and her coldness looks different beside them. She remembers Bridget tenderly ("Clever hands"), and recalls the girl who "sang at the copper, which I let her do". Her aside that "there's no rule against a song, God knows, / though there is one against its being heard" is bitterly ironic. She knows servants may have inner lives only so long as nobody hears them.

The strongest pull towards sympathy is her admission that keeping "my counsel" is "the hardest keeping". It concedes a guilt she cannot act on, and the copper still "singing" on wash-days suggests she is haunted by Bridget's absence. The steam, "thick and low", blocks sight, much like the moral fog she lives in.

In the end, the form makes sympathy hard to hold back, because she gives away more of her conscience than she means to. She isn't innocent. The poem suggests, though, that her silence is produced by a system that punishes speech, so we judge the household more harshly than the woman who serves it.

sets.title: In Defence of Boredom
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original personal essay. The writer is fictional.
sets.body:
When I was nine, the most boring place in the world was my grandmother's lounge room in Launceston on a Sunday afternoon. There was a clock that ticked as if it were being paid by the tick. There was a bowl of wax fruit nobody was allowed to touch. There was a television, but it lived under a crocheted cover, like a budgie that had been put to bed. And there was me, on the carpet, with nothing to do for three hours while the adults talked about people who had died.

I want to say clearly, before I go on, that I hated it. I am not one of those people who looks back on childhood suffering and calls it character. I was bored to the point of physical pain. I counted the squares in the carpet pattern. I tried to read the newspaper upside down. I lay on my back and stared at the ceiling until the light fitting began to look like a jellyfish, and then like a face, and then like a map of an island that does not exist, which I named and populated and governed, with some cruelty, for the rest of the afternoon.

That island, it turns out, is the reason I am a writer.

I have been thinking about this because I have not been bored, properly bored, in perhaps eleven years. I have a phone. You have a phone. Between us we have abolished the waiting room, the bus stop, the queue at the bank, the ten minutes before a film starts. Every gap in the day now has something in it, the way every gap in a cheap wall has filler. I can no longer remember the last time I stared at a ceiling long enough for it to become anything other than a ceiling.

The usual way to argue this is with research, and there is research, though I am suspicious of anyone who tells you that a study has proved something about your soul. So let me argue it the other way, from the carpet. Boredom is not empty. Boredom is the feeling of your mind discovering that nobody is going to entertain it, and deciding, slowly and resentfully, to entertain itself. It is the dull grey waiting room outside imagination. You cannot get into the room without sitting in the waiting room first.

I do not want to romanticise this. Boredom is also what happens to people in jobs that grind them down, in hospitals, in detention, in lives with no doors in them. That boredom is not a gift. It is a wound, and nobody should be told to be grateful for it. The boredom I am defending is a smaller and more privileged thing: the bored afternoon that has an end.

But I think it is worth defending. Last month, on a delayed train, my phone died. For forty minutes I looked out of the window at the backs of houses, their washing lines and trampolines and bins. Around the twentieth minute, something unlocked. I began to wonder about the people who lived there, and then to invent them, and by the time the train moved I had the first page of a story.

My grandmother's clock is in my hallway now. It still ticks as if it is being paid by the tick. I have never once wanted to throw it out.

questions.model:
The tone moves from comic nostalgia to reflection, then to sober qualification, and finally to quiet affirmation. Each shift makes the defence of boredom more believable.

The opening is playful. The clock ticks "as if it were being paid by the tick" and the television sits under its cover "like a budgie that had been put to bed"; the exaggeration makes the grandmother's lounge room comically dead, so we suffer along with the child. Then the writer insists "that I hated it". Refusing to sentimentalise earns our trust before the argument has even started.

The one-line paragraph "That island, it turns out, is the reason I am a writer" changes the tone to revelation. What follows is direct and inclusive: "I have a phone. You have a phone." The parallel sentences pull the reader in, and comparing constant stimulation to filler in "every gap in a cheap wall" makes it seem shoddy.

The biggest shift is into seriousness: "I do not want to romanticise this." The writer admits that boredom in "detention" or in "lives with no doors in them" is "a wound". This sober concession narrows the claim to "the bored afternoon that has an end", which makes the argument more precise and harder to dismiss.

The ending settles into warmth. The clock still ticks "as if it is being paid by the tick", echoing the opening, but now fondly: "I have never once wanted to throw it out." Coming full circle shows the writer's attitude has changed, which is the argument in miniature: boredom, remembered, turns out to be valuable.

questions.model:
I find the defence of boredom largely convincing. The writer argues from vivid personal evidence, defines the key term honestly and deals with the strongest objection. The case is limited, though, by resting on one kind of experience, which the writer openly admits is a privileged one.

The essay's biggest strength is that it shows the process it defends instead of just asserting it. Staring at the ceiling, the writer watches the light fitting become "like a jellyfish, and then like a face, and then like a map of an island that does not exist". The sentence keeps adding images, so we watch imagination arrive in real time. By the time we read "That island, it turns out, is the reason I am a writer", the conclusion feels earned.

The redefinition of boredom is also persuasive. It is not "empty" but "the feeling of your mind discovering that nobody is going to entertain it", and "the dull grey waiting room outside imagination" captures both its discomfort and its purpose. "You cannot get into the room without sitting in the waiting room first" is memorable, but it is a claim, not something the essay proves.

The handling of objections adds credibility. The writer is suspicious of research that claims to have "proved something about your soul" and prefers to argue "from the carpet", which some readers will see as dodging the evidence. More persuasive is the concession that for people in grinding jobs or "detention" boredom "is a wound". Limiting the case to "the bored afternoon that has an end" stops the essay from sounding glib.

Its weakness is that the evidence is anecdotal, and it comes from a writer, someone already inclined to value letting the mind drift. The train story, where the "first page of a story" turns up after forty minutes, may not move a reader who simply finds boredom unpleasant.

So the essay convinces me as a reflective argument rather than a proof. Its candour, its imagery and its careful limits make a modest claim persuasively, even if they can't support a universal one.

sets.title: The Last Milk Bar on Ferris Street
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original feature article. The people, the shop and the suburb are fictional.
sets.body:
At 6.15 every morning, Eleni Kostas turns the sign on the door of the Ferris Street Milk Bar from CLOSED to OPEN, and then, because the hinge is loose, she turns it back again with her thumb so it stays straight. She has done this for forty-three years. 'The sign is older than my son,' she says. 'It complains more, too.'

The milk bar sits on the corner of Ferris and Dunn streets, in a suburb that has changed around it like water around a stone. The fruit shop is now a pilates studio. The bank is a café that serves coffee in jars. Across the road, a supermarket with self-service lanes and a car park the size of a football field opened six years ago. And still, every morning, a small queue forms outside Eleni's door: tradies wanting pies, schoolkids wanting mixed lollies, an elderly man who wants nothing but the newspaper and ten minutes of conversation about the football.

Milk bars were once everywhere in Australian suburbs, many of them run by migrant families, Greek and Italian especially, who worked long hours behind counters stacked with sweets and magazines. Most have now closed. Eleni knows she is something of a survivor. She does not seem to find it romantic.

'People come in and take photos,' she says, wiping down a counter that is already clean. 'They say, oh, it's so nostalgic. Then they go and buy their milk at the supermarket.' She shrugs. 'Nostalgia doesn't pay the electricity.'

Her husband, Kostas, died fifteen years ago. (Yes, she says, laughing, she married a man whose first name was her surname. 'Everybody in the village thought it was very efficient.') Since then she has run the shop alone, with occasional help from her granddaughter, Sofia, who is nineteen and studying engineering.

Sofia has opinions about the business. She has set up a card machine, an Instagram account and a spreadsheet. 'Yiayia's system was a notebook,' she says. 'Which was actually incredible. She knew every customer's tab to the cent. But you can't sell a notebook.'

Is she going to take over? Sofia laughs, then stops laughing. 'I don't know,' she says. 'I love it. But I don't want to love it the way she loves it. She hasn't had a holiday since 1994.'

What keeps people coming back is difficult to measure. Tom Le, a plumber who has stopped here every working day for a decade, struggles to explain. 'The pies are fine,' he says. 'They're not the best pies.' He thinks. 'She asked about my daughter when she was sick. Every day. Even after she was better, Eleni still asked. You don't get that at the servo.'

At closing time, Eleni counts the till by hand, though the card machine has already done it for her. She saves the coins in a biscuit tin for her grandchildren. When I ask what will happen to the shop when she retires, she looks at me as if I have asked something faintly rude.

'Retire,' she says, trying the word like an unfamiliar sweet. Then she turns the sign. It swings crooked. She leaves it.

sets.title: A Letter from the Diggings, 1853
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original text written in the style of a mid-nineteenth-century letter. The writer, Mary Treloar, is fictional. She writes from the Victorian goldfields to her sister Jane in Redruth, Cornwall.
sets.body:
Forest Creek, the 14th of March, 1853

My dear Jane,

I take up my pen at last, having owed you this letter since Christmas, and having begun it, I confess, four times, and four times put it in the stove. You will forgive me when I tell you that it is no easy thing to describe a place to one who has never left Redruth, and harder still to describe it truthfully to one who will read the letter aloud at chapel.

You asked in your last whether the streets here are paved with gold. They are not paved at all. When it rains, which it has done these nine days without mercy, the whole of the Creek becomes one sucking mire, and I have seen a dray sink to its axles before the very door of our tent, and the bullocks stand in it groaning like Methodists at a funeral. When it is dry the dust gets into the bread, into the bedding, into the very pages of the Bible, so that I cannot open Ruth without a little cloud rising out of her.

Thomas is well, or says he is. He goes down the shaft at first light and comes up at dusk the colour of the earth, so that I know him only by his voice and his way of standing. We have had some colour, a few grains in December and a little more in January, enough to keep us in flour and tea and hope, though hope is dearer here than either. There are men about us who have made their fortunes in a week, and men who have dug for a year and found nothing but water, and the lucky and the unlucky drink together of a Saturday at the same sly-grog tent, so that you cannot tell by looking which is which until the fighting starts.

I will not pretend to you that I am happy, Jane, but neither will I pretend that I am sorry we came. There is a freedom in it that I cannot well explain. No one here asks whose daughter I am. The woman in the next tent is from Kilkenny, and the man across the gully is a Chinese gentleman who grows cabbages better than any in Cornwall and sells them to me at a fair price and bows when I pay him, which is more than the grocer at home ever did.

Do not read that part aloud.

The nights are the worst of it. The sky is too large and the stars are in the wrong places, and I lie awake and think of the lane behind Mother's, and the smell of the rain coming in from the sea, which here comes from nowhere, there being no sea, only the bush, which goes on and on and does not care whether we are in it.

Tell Mother we are prospering. It is very nearly true. Tell her that I wear my good shawl to chapel, which is a tent like the rest, and that the minister is a Wesleyan of sound views. Tell her nothing of the mire.

I enclose a grain of gold that Thomas found on my birthday. It is very small. Hold it to the window and you will see it is the same colour as the light.

Your loving sister,
Mary

She takes the cliché in Jane's question literally and rejects it: the streets are not paved with gold, "They are not paved at all." That blunt short sentence punctures the fantasy before she offers the replacement, "one sucking mire" in which a dray sinks "to its axles". Mud, not romance. Her similes translate the strange place into things her Cornish readers know, and that makes it absurd: the bullocks "stand in it groaning like Methodists at a funeral", and the dust gets everywhere, so that "I cannot open Ruth without a little cloud rising out of her." Turning the book of Ruth into a person is witty, but it also hints that even faith gets coated by the new country. Then she unsettles the idea of fortune itself. There are "men about us who have made their fortunes in a week, and men who have dug for a year and found nothing but water", and the balanced sentence makes success look completely random. You "cannot tell by looking which is which until the fighting starts", which wrecks any picture of an orderly, prosperous colony. Her readers are left seeing the goldfields as a lottery played in mud.

Mary records hardship frankly, but she frames it so that a guarded celebration of freedom becomes the emotional centre of the letter. The celebration is real, yet it is private, held back by homesickness and by the need to hide it from home. The letter is best read as a negotiation between the two rather than a straightforward triumph.

The hardship is vivid, sometimes comic. The rain has fallen "these nine days without mercy", the Creek is "one sucking mire", and Thomas comes up from the shaft "the colour of the earth, so that I know him only by his voice and his way of standing." That image suggests the diggings strip away identity as well as comfort. Her remark that hope is "dearer here than either" flour or tea borrows the language of prices to measure emotional cost.

Against this, Mary makes a careful case for freedom. "I will not pretend to you that I am happy, Jane, but neither will I pretend that I am sorry we came" refuses both false cheer and complaint. She admits, "There is a freedom in it that I cannot well explain", and the freedom she means is escape from the class and family hierarchy of Redruth: "No one here asks whose daughter I am." Her respect for the gardener who "bows when I pay him" extends this to freedom of judgement, and that is immediately fenced off by the one-line paragraph "Do not read that part aloud."

That instruction marks the limit of the celebration. She also manages what her mother knows ("Tell Mother we are prospering. It is very nearly true") and is homesick at night, when "the stars are in the wrong places" and the bush "does not care whether we are in it". Freedom here comes bundled with exposure.

The final image gathers these tensions. The grain of gold is "very small", an honest admission that success has been modest, yet Jane will see "it is the same colour as the light." Its value lies in connection rather than money, joining two sisters under one light. So the letter does celebrate freedom to a considerable extent, but quietly, as something only a sister can be trusted to see.

sets.title: The Water Line
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an original memoir extract about a flood in a northern New South Wales river town. Text 2 is an original poem. The town and its pub are fictional.
sets.body:
After the water went down, my mother walked through the house with a pencil, marking the line it had left on every wall.

She did this before she cried, before she rang the insurance, before she so much as lifted the sodden rug in the hall. Room by room she found the brown tidemark the river had drawn at the height of her shoulders, and she traced it, carefully, as if the house were a child she was measuring against a doorframe. In the kitchen it ran straight through the calendar, so that every day in March was cut in half.

'Why are you doing that?' I asked. I was sixteen and I had come home from my aunt's in borrowed gumboots, and I wanted her to stop being calm.

'So we remember,' she said.

'We're not going to forget.'

'You'd be surprised,' she said, and went on into the laundry.

Everything below the line was ruined. Everything above it was fine, and that was the strangest part: the clock still ticking above the stove, my school certificates dry in their frames, the top shelf of the pantry with its tins of peaches standing in a neat row as if nothing had happened, while beneath them the flour had become a grey paste that smelled like a creek bed. The house had been divided into before and after, horizontally.

For weeks the street was a line of furniture. Couches, mattresses, a piano with its lid sprung open like a mouth. Volunteers came from towns I had only seen on maps and carried our lives out to the kerb and were kind about it. A woman in a hi-vis vest held up a photograph album, swollen to twice its size, and looked at me with a question, and I said yes, throw it out, and then ran after the truck.

We painted the walls in May. My mother chose a colour called Linen White. Before the first coat went on, she took the pencil and wrote the date beside the line in the hallway, small, behind where the coat hooks would go, where no one would look.

It is still there. She has painted over it twice. You can see it if you know where it is, a faint grey ridge under the white, like a scar that has learned to keep quiet.

pair.title: High-Water Mark
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
On the pub wall in town there is a ladder
of floods, painted in neat black capitals:
1954 at the height of a man's chin,
1974 a hand above it,
and the new one, still unpainted, a stain
the publican has circled with a texta
and will not let anyone clean.

We stand under them with our beers
and read them like a family tree,
the old men pointing, I was here for that one,
and that one, and that,
as if each year were a relative
who came to stay and wouldn't leave.

Nobody mentions the gap between them,
the forty years of ordinary weather,
of dry Christmases, of the river
lying low and brown and harmless as a dog
asleep in the sun across the doorway,
the dog you step over every morning
until you forget that it has teeth.

questions.model:
Both texts suggest that remembering a disaster doesn't simply follow from surviving it. It is a deliberate act that has to be repeated against the pull of forgetting, and the marks people make both honour what they endured and warn about what might come back.

Each text centres on a record of the water's height. In Text 1 the mother traces the tidemark "Room by room", and her short exchange with her daughter states the purpose outright: "So we remember." When the daughter says "We're not going to forget", the answer, "You'd be surprised", predicts exactly the danger Text 2 dramatises. In the poem the flood heights are painted on the pub wall in "neat black capitals", a public record the publican protects by refusing to let anyone clean the latest stain.

The kind of memory differs, though. In Text 1 it is private and restrained. The mother writes the date "small", where "no one would look", and the closing simile of the line beneath the paint, "like a scar that has learned to keep quiet", presents memory as a wound that has healed without disappearing. In Text 2 memory is communal and almost sociable: the drinkers read the marks "like a family tree" and the old men point and boast. Disaster turns into folklore.

Read side by side, each text explains something the other leaves unsaid. The poem's last stanza shows why the mother's pencil matters: over "forty years of ordinary weather" the river comes to seem "harmless as a dog", and people "forget that it has teeth". The memoir, in turn, supplies what the pub-wall stories leave out: the ruined flour, the swollen photo album, the private grief that won't fit on a public wall.

Together, then, the texts suggest that the memory of disaster has to be kept in two forms: a quiet, private mark that holds on to what it cost, and a public story that keeps its warning alive. Either on its own is incomplete. Together they resist the comfortable forgetting both texts fear.

sets.title: Cicada Shells
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original free-verse poem. Cicadas leave their empty outer skins (shells) on tree bark when they emerge as adults in summer.
sets.body:
All January the shells hung on the paperbark
by our back fence, a dozen at a time,
hooked to the soft bark by their small brown claws
as if they had stopped there to rest
and would be going on in a minute.

My brother collected them in a jam jar.
He said they were dead. I said they were empty,
which isn't the same, and we fought about it
the way you fight at ten, with your whole body,
till our mother came out and said
they were neither, they were left.

Each one split cleanly down the back,
a door that only opens once.
You could see where the thing had pulled itself out,
wet and folded, into the heat,
and sat a whole morning drying its wings
before it could stand to be what it was.

The noise they made was the noise of the summer itself,
so loud it was a kind of silence,
so constant we forgot to hear it
until the evening in February it stopped.

My brother is taller than our father now.
He doesn't remember the jar.
Some mornings I look at him across the kitchen
and see the line down the back of the boy he was,
the place where the man climbed out,
and the shell of him still hanging somewhere,

questions.model: In this poem time passes almost without anyone noticing, and it is only seen afterwards, through images of motion that seems paused and a sound so constant it disappears. In the first stanza the shells look "as if they had stopped there to rest / and would be going on in a minute". It's an image of time on hold, and it's ironic, because the moment of change has already happened. The fourth stanza builds on this with a paradox: the cicadas were "so loud it was a kind of silence, / so constant we forgot to hear it". The repeated "so" imitates the drone, and the paradox suggests that whatever fills every moment of a childhood summer is exactly what nobody hears. The stanza's last line, "until the evening in February it stopped", makes us register the sound only once it's gone, just as the speaker did. The structure then gives us the same jolt. The final stanza jumps years with no transition: "My brother is taller than our father now." Growing up seems to have happened offstage, in the gap between stanzas, the way the cicadas' song ended before anyone noticed it was ending.

questions.model:
The cicada works very well as an extended metaphor because the poem builds it slowly, from a children's argument about empty shells to an adult realising his brother has left a former self behind. By the end, the meaning has been earned rather than announced.

The first stanza makes the shells eerily lifelike. Hooked onto the paperbark "by their small brown claws", they look "as if they had stopped there to rest / and would be going on in a minute." The irony is gentle. We know they won't go on, and the idea is planted of a self that looks present but has already moved out.

The second stanza turns description into argument. The children's fight over whether the shells are "dead" or "empty" acts out two ways of seeing change, as loss or as departure, and the mother's "they were neither, they were left" gives the metaphor its key word. If something is left, someone has gone on living elsewhere.

The third stanza gives the change emotional weight. The split "down the back" becomes "a door that only opens once", so growing up can't be undone. The creature is vulnerable, "wet and folded", and sits "a whole morning drying its wings / before it could stand to be what it was". Maturity has to be grown into, even endured, and "stand to be" works both physically and emotionally.

The last stanza applies the metaphor directly, which could have felt heavy-handed, but the restraint saves it. "He doesn't remember the jar" is a plain statement, and it lets us feel what the speaker has kept and the brother has lost. "the line down the back of the boy he was" merges brother and cicada, and the shell "holding on to the bark with both hands" flips our expectations: it is the abandoned childhood self, not the adult, that clings on. Because each stanza adds something new to the same image, the metaphor is precise, moving and coherent.

sets.title: The Night the Pobblebonks Came Back
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original hybrid text: a volunteer's blog post that embeds a transcript of an audio recording and readers' comments. The blogger, the commenters and the website are fictional. The eastern banjo frog is commonly called the pobblebonk because of its call.
sets.body:
FROGWATCH ILLAWARRA: a volunteer's notebook
Post 214: The Night the Pobblebonks Came Back
Posted by Margaret (Marg) Hollis | 3 comments

I have been sitting beside the same dam on the edge of the escarpment every second Tuesday for eleven years. I bring a folding chair, a thermos, a torch with a red filter so I don't dazzle anyone, and my phone, which records for exactly ten minutes while I sit very still and try not to cough. Then I come home and listen to the recording with headphones and write down who was there.

People ask what I'm counting. I'm not counting frogs, exactly. I'm counting voices. A frog you can hear is a frog that is alive, and a frog that is calling is a frog that thinks there's a future worth calling into.

For the last three years the dam has been mostly striped marsh frogs, which sound like someone dropping a tennis ball on a wooden floor, and the odd common eastern froglet going crick-crick-crick in the reeds. Nothing wrong with them. But the eastern banjo frog, the pobblebonk, the one that goes bonk like a plucked string, had gone. After the dry years I'd stopped expecting it. I'd started writing 'nil' in that column without really listening.

Here is last Tuesday's recording, as best I can transcribe it.

[AUDIO TRANSCRIPT: Dam 3, 8:42 pm, light rain, 14°C]
00:00 wind; my chair creaks (sorry)
00:12 striped marsh frog: tok... tok... tok
00:47 froglets, several, overlapping: crick-crick-crick-crick
02:30 car on the road above; everything stops
03:05 froglets resume, then marsh frogs
05:58 [faint, far side of dam] bonk
06:01 bonk
06:03 me, under my breath: oh. oh, hello.
06:10 bonk... bonk... [a second animal answers] bonk
09:50 rain gets heavier; recording ends

I listened to 05:58 about forty times. I'm not ashamed to say I cried a bit at the kitchen table, which my husband pretended not to notice, and then he came and listened too.

Two pobblebonks. That is the data. It doesn't mean the catchment has recovered or that anyone should stop worrying about the developers' plans for the ridge. It means that two frogs, on one wet night, decided the dam was worth singing to. I've logged it with the council's database, and I've written it here, because a number in a spreadsheet doesn't tell you what it sounds like when something you'd given up on answers.

Bring a chair next time. Bring a thermos. Sit still.

COMMENTS (3)

Dev_K: Marg, this made my week. Heard one at Dam 7 on Saturday and didn't log it because I thought I'd imagined it. Logging it now.

lyrebird_lou: The bit where you say 'oh, hello' is the whole reason I volunteer.

Council Environment Team: Thanks Margaret, record received and verified. Great work.

Giving the frogs a sense of hope turns their calls into a measure of how healthy the place is, and of optimism itself. That prepares us for the climax. When the pobblebonk calls, it's a voice, not a statistic, and her whispered "oh, hello" turns the count into a conversation with "something you'd given up on".

questions.model:
Moving from blog to transcript to comments, the post takes the reader from explanation to experience to community, so the pobblebonks' return is felt as an event rather than reported as a fact.

The blog section sets up Marg's credibility and patience. Her routine, "every second Tuesday for eleven years", with its red-filtered torch and ten-minute recording, shows a disciplined observer, and her admission that she had been writing nil "in that column without really listening" sets up a turn. We're ready for a lapse in attention to be corrected.

The transcript then switches from telling to evidence. Its bracketed conditions, "8:42 pm, light rain, 14°C", look like a scientific record, and the onomatopoeia ("tok... tok... tok", "crick-crick-crick-crick") lets us hear the dam's everyday chorus. Because the transcript unfolds in time, we wait with her: at 02:30 a car passes and "everything stops", which builds tension, so the faint "bonk" at 05:58 comes as a real surprise. Her whispered "oh. oh, hello." breaks the record's neutrality, and we see the exact moment data becomes emotion.

The comments widen the meaning. Dev_K decides to log a call he "thought I'd imagined", so the post is already changing what people do; lyrebird_lou calls Marg's greeting "the whole reason I volunteer"; and the council's flat "record received and verified" reminds us of the official system that, as Marg says, can't capture "what it sounds like". Together the three forms make us value the frogs' return as both verified data and shared joy.

questions.model:
The post balances scientific restraint and personal feeling with real skill, and the balance is more than a question of tone. It is the post's argument: careful observation and emotional response are both ways of knowing, and each makes the other believable.

Marg's restraint comes from her method. Her routine, "every second Tuesday for eleven years", and the transcript's timestamps mark her as a disciplined citizen scientist. Even at the climax she sticks to precision: "Two pobblebonks. That is the data." Those clipped fragments refuse to exaggerate, and she qualifies the finding straight away: "It doesn't mean the catchment has recovered or that anyone should stop worrying about the developers' plans for the ridge." The caution protects her credibility and keeps her campaign for the ridge going without any shouting.

The feeling runs through the restraint rather than against it. Inside the transcript her whisper, "oh. oh, hello.", breaks the neutral record, and admitting she listened "about forty times" uses a number to measure emotion. Self-mocking understatement keeps sentiment in check: she "cried a bit at the kitchen table, which my husband pretended not to notice". The humour makes the emotion believable rather than performed.

One sentence joins the two modes. Having given the data, she reads it again: "two frogs, on one wet night, decided the dam was worth singing to." The personification isn't scientific, but it follows from her earlier claim that a calling frog "thinks there's a future worth calling into". Then she justifies the post itself. The record is logged with the council, but she writes "because a number in a spreadsheet doesn't tell you what it sounds like". She isn't rejecting data; she's arguing that data needs a voice.

The ending confirms the balance. "Bring a chair next time. Bring a thermos. Sit still." turns method into an invitation, and the council's "record received and verified" sits beside lyrebird_lou's delight. The post succeeds: its restraint earns our trust, and its feeling gives that trust a purpose.

sets.title: Built for the Long Way Round
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original magazine advertisement for a fictional car brand. A description of the image is given in square brackets. The owner quoted is fictional.
sets.body:
[Full-page magazine advertisement. Image: a red four-wheel drive parked alone on a salt lake at dawn. No people are visible.]

HEADLINE
Somewhere out there, your phone has no signal.
Good.

BODY COPY
You remember the last time you were unreachable. Maybe you were nine, and the creek was the whole world. Maybe you were nineteen, and the road was. Then life got busy. Then it got loud.

The all-new Kestrel Ridgeline was built for the moment you take it back.

Permanent four-wheel drive that reads the ground before you do. A 900-kilometre range, so the next servo is a suggestion, not a plan. Leather seats that remember how you like to sit, and a cabin so quiet you can finally hear yourself think. (We checked. You have some good ideas.)

And when you need the world again, it's right there: 12.3-inch touchscreen, wireless smartphone mirroring, and a satellite emergency beacon, standard. Because freedom is better when someone knows where you are.

Out there, nobody asks what you do for a living. The salt doesn't care about your inbox. The horizon has never once scheduled a meeting.

Go further. Come back different.

OWNER STORY
'Three weeks to the Gulf and back. I checked my email once, in Normanton, and then I turned the phone off again.' Kestrel owner, Toowoomba

KESTREL RIDGELINE
Built for the long way round.

FINE PRINT
Kestrel Ridgeline GXL shown with optional Adventure Pack. Drive-away pricing from $78,990. Range based on laboratory testing; actual range will vary with driving conditions, load and terrain. Off-road driving should only be undertaken by experienced drivers on legally accessible tracks. Do not drive on salt lakes; vehicle shown on a closed set. Satellite beacon requires an active subscription after 12 months.

The joke that "The horizon has never once scheduled a meeting" plays on their sense of being trapped by office life, and the car becomes an escape they can afford.

questions.model:
The freedom this ad sells is escape from the noise and obligations of adult working life, and it's a freedom you can buy back.

The headline starts the job: "Somewhere out there, your phone has no signal." We expect that to be a worry, but the one-word sentence "Good." flips it, so being disconnected becomes a luxury. The image backs this up, a car "parked alone on a salt lake at dawn" where "No people are visible". Freedom looks like solitude and empty space.

The body copy then treats freedom as something the reader has lost. "Maybe you were nine, and the creek was the whole world. Maybe you were nineteen, and the road was." The parallel sentences, addressed straight to "you", trade on nostalgia, and "Then life got busy. Then it got loud." squeezes adulthood into a decline. The car is the remedy, "built for the moment you take it back", and "take it back" turns freedom into a possession you can reclaim.

Even the technical features are converted into feelings. The fuel range means "the next servo is a suggestion, not a plan", so a specification becomes spontaneity, and the quiet cabin lets you "finally hear yourself think". The aside "(We checked. You have some good ideas.)" flatters the reader. Personification sharpens the contrast with the office: "The salt doesn't care about your inbox."

The ending, "Go further. Come back different." and the tagline "Built for the long way round.", presents freedom as transformation, but on a round trip. What's on offer is temporary, safe and for sale: an escape that always comes home.
