questions.model:
Taken literally, the ad contradicts its promise of escape again and again. Those contradictions aren't a failure of the copy, though. They show what it is really selling: the feeling of escape without the risks. So the contradiction is extensive, but carefully managed.

The promise is extravagant. The headline celebrates "no signal", and we're told "Out there, nobody asks what you do for a living." Yet the same copy reassures us that "when you need the world again, it's right there", then lists a "12.3-inch touchscreen, wireless smartphone mirroring, and a satellite emergency beacon", reinstalling the exact devices the headline threw away. "freedom is better when someone knows where you are" is a paradox that admits the audience doesn't want real isolation. They want solitude with a safety net.

The fine print goes further. The range that made servos "a suggestion" is "based on laboratory testing", and a car that "reads the ground before you do" sits awkwardly next to the warning that off-road driving is only for "experienced drivers on legally accessible tracks". Most strikingly, the central image falls apart: "Do not drive on salt lakes; vehicle shown on a closed set." The wilderness was staged. Even safety turns into an ongoing payment, because the beacon "requires an active subscription after 12 months".

Do these contradictions weaken the ad? Not necessarily. Fine print is designed to be skimmed, and the warm "you" voice and nostalgic appeals have done their emotional work before anyone reaches the qualifications. The audience being flattered, professionals who can afford "$78,990", may also knowingly accept a curated, temporary escape; "Go further. Come back different" promises a return as much as a departure.

In fact, then, the ad contradicts its promise almost completely, while keeping it alive in feeling. A critical reader sees that the product isn't freedom but a reassuring picture of it.

sets.title: It's Not Cold
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original eulogy, delivered by a former swimmer at the funeral of a swimming-pool coach in a country town. The speaker, the coach and the town of Yarrumba are fictional.
sets.body:
Lorna Pike taught half this town to swim, and she taught the other half to stop complaining about the cold.

If you grew up in Yarrumba, you know the sound I mean: a whistle at six in the morning, so loud the magpies left the pool fence, and a voice behind it saying, 'It's not cold. You're just not moving yet.' I heard that sentence four hundred times between the ages of seven and seventeen. I believed it about twice.

Lorna ran the pool for thirty-one summers. She opened it in October, when the water was still green at the deep end, and she closed it in March, when the last of us had stopped turning up. In between she ran learn-to-swim for the toddlers, squad for the keen kids, aqua aerobics for the ladies from the CWA, and a Tuesday night session for adults who had never learned and were too embarrassed to say so. She never told anyone who came to the Tuesday nights. Some of them are here today. You know who you are. She kept your secret, and so will I.

She was not a soft woman. She would tell you your tumble turn looked like a dropped wardrobe. She would tell your parents, too. But if you were the kid whose family couldn't pay for the season pass, you would find, somehow, that your name was already on the list, and if you asked about it she would look at you as if you'd said something in Latin.

I want to tell you about one morning. I was twelve, and I had come last in the district carnival by the length of a whole pool, and I had decided I was finished with swimming forever. I sat in the change rooms in my towel and would not come out. Lorna didn't come in after me. She just stood outside the door and talked about the weather for twenty minutes, the drought, the price of chlorine, the new council, until I came out because I was bored. Then she handed me a kickboard and said, 'Two laps. Nobody's watching.' Nobody was. It was the best swim of my life.

That was her method. She didn't fix you. She waited beside you until you were ready to move, and then she made sure you had something to hold on to.

The council has asked me to say that the pool will be renamed in her honour, and I'm glad. But I think Lorna would want something harder than a sign. She would want the pool open in October, green water and all. She would want the Tuesday nights to keep going. She would want somebody standing on the edge at six in the morning with a whistle and a terrible joke, telling some shivering kid it's not cold.

So here is what I am asking. If she taught you, teach someone. If she kept your secret, keep somebody else's. And when you go past the pool this summer and hear that whistle, and you will hear it, whoever is blowing it, get in.

It's not cold. You're just not moving yet.

She waited beside you until you were ready to move". Giving a child "something to hold on to", like a kickboard, turns one memory into a portrait of how Lorna always worked.

questions.model:
Over the speech, Lorna's catchphrase grows from a remembered joke into a principle for living, and finally into an instruction to the grieving town, so the speech ends with Lorna's voice speaking again.

At first the phrase is comic characterisation. Alongside "a whistle at six in the morning, so loud the magpies left the pool fence", the line "It's not cold. You're just not moving yet." captures her brisk, unsentimental toughness. The speaker's aside, "I heard that sentence four hundred times between the ages of seven and seventeen. I believed it about twice.", gets a laugh from everyone who heard it too.

The change-room story then shows the philosophy inside the joke. The speaker boils Lorna's method down in short statements: "She didn't fix you. She waited beside you until you were ready to move". The word "move" links straight back to the catchphrase. Discomfort isn't denied; it's overcome by doing something, not by being rescued.

In the last section the phrase becomes a call to action. The repeated "She would want" builds the idea of a living memorial, "something harder than a sign", and "If she taught you, teach someone. If she kept your secret, keep somebody else's." turns gratitude into obligation through parallel commands. The blunt "get in." applies the old poolside order to the whole community.

Finally the speaker ends on the catchphrase itself, and its meaning has grown. The cold is now grief, and moving means carrying on Lorna's work. Coming full circle lets the speech finish in her own words, so she comforts and challenges the mourners one last time.

sets.title: Figures Do Not Have Names
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an original speech written in the style of the early 1930s, when many Australians were unemployed during the Great Depression; the speaker is fictional. Text 2 is an original feature article extract about a food-delivery rider; the rider, the journalist and the platform are fictional.
sets.body:
Speech at a meeting of the unemployed, the Domain, Sydney, 1931

Friends, and I call you friends, for there is no other word for men who have stood in the same queue since daylight:

They tell us that there is no work. I say there is work enough in this city for every pair of hands in this park. There are roads unmade and houses unbuilt and children unfed, and there are men here who can make and build and feed, and the only thing that stands between the two is a ledger in a bank in Pitt Street.

They tell us to be patient. We have been patient. We were patient in the trenches, where we were told we were fighting for a better world. We were patient at the wharves and in the shearing sheds, where we were told the good times were coming. Patience, friends, is a fine virtue in a man with a full belly. In a man with hungry children it begins to look very like surrender.

They tell us that we are a burden. Look about you. Look at the man beside you. That man laid the bricks of the very building where they tell him he is a burden. That man's hands drove the rivets of the bridge they are so proud of. There is not a stone in this city that was not lifted by somebody's father.

I do not ask for charity. Charity is what is given to a man you have decided is less than yourself. I ask for work, and wages for work, and the plain respect that is owed to any man who will put his back to a load.

And I say this to the gentlemen in their offices, who will read of this meeting in tomorrow's papers: you may count us as figures in your columns. But figures do not stand in the rain. Figures do not have names. Every man here has a name, and before this winter is out, by God, you shall learn some of them.

pair.title: The App Doesn't Know His Name
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
It is 9.40 pm on a Friday in Parramatta, and Arjun has been riding since eleven this morning. His phone is clamped to the handlebars of a second-hand e-bike, and every few minutes it chimes, a bright, cheerful sound, like a game show contestant getting an answer right. Each chime is an offer: a burger, four kilometres, $6.80. He has fifteen seconds to accept.

'If you say no too many times,' he says, 'it stops asking.'

Arjun is twenty-six. In Hyderabad he studied civil engineering. Here, he is what the platform calls an independent contractor, which means he supplies the bike, the phone, the insurance and the body, and the app supplies the work, when it chooses to. He doesn't have a manager. He has a rating: 4.91 out of five. He knows the number the way other people know their height.

Nobody has ever been rude to him, exactly. That is part of the strangeness. The customers he delivers to mostly don't look at him at all; they take the bag at the door with their eyes on a screen, or they have left instructions to leave it on the mat and not to knock. Once, a woman in Westmead came out to the gate in her dressing gown with a glass of water, because it was thirty-eight degrees. He still talks about her. He doesn't know her name either.

The platform, in a statement, said that riders 'value the flexibility' of the work and that its pay model 'reflects market conditions'. Both of these things may be true. Arjun does value the flexibility; it lets him study for his engineering accreditation in the mornings. And the market conditions are certainly reflected, in the way a puddle reflects the sky.

At 10.15 the chime comes again. A bubble tea, two kilometres, $5.20. He taps accept before I can ask whether it's worth it.

'Everything is worth it,' he says, pulling his helmet on, 'until you add it up.'

Then he is gone into the traffic, a small green light among the red ones, and somewhere a restaurant tablet is already printing his first name.

Against the claim that there is no work, he sets "roads unmade and houses unbuilt and children unfed", and argues the only thing in the way is "a ledger in a bank in Pitt Street", a metonym that shrinks power down to cold bookkeeping. He redefines patience by contrast: a virtue "in a man with a full belly", it "begins to look very like surrender" when you're hungry. And when the unemployed are called "a burden", he turns to the crowd itself: "Look at the man beside you". These are the men whose labour built the city. Every claim ends up turned back on the people who made it.

The app's chime sounds like "a game show contestant getting an answer right", and the cheerful simile is ironic, because it covers the pressure of an offer he has "fifteen seconds to accept". He has a rating" put a number where a relationship should be, a number he knows "the way other people know their height". questions.text: Compare how Text 1 and Text 2 represent the dignity of work and what threatens it.

questions.model:
Both texts insist that work has a dignity, and that the dignity is threatened when people are turned into numbers. They place the threat differently, though. Text 1 confronts a system that withholds work from people who want it; Text 2 looks at a system that hands out work while withholding recognition. Read together, they suggest dignity depends less on having a job than on being known.

Both set names against figures. In Text 1 the speaker warns the "gentlemen in their offices" that "figures do not stand in the rain. Figures do not have names", and his closing threat, "you shall learn some of them", treats identity as a kind of power. In Text 2 the figures have won. Arjun has "a rating: 4.91 out of five" instead of a manager, and the article closes on a tablet printing only "his first name". Even his one human moment ends with "He doesn't know her name either."

Both also place power in distant, abstract systems. Text 1's "ledger in a bank in Pitt Street" looks ahead to Text 2's app, which hands out work "when it chooses to". Each text exposes official language. The speaker mocks the refrain "They tell us", while the journalist quotes the platform's claim that riders "value the flexibility" and undercuts its "market conditions" with the dry simile "in the way a puddle reflects the sky".

Where they differ most is in voice and response. Text 1 is collective and oratorical: its inclusive "we", its demand for "work, and wages for work, and the plain respect", and its oath "by God" are built to move a crowd to act. Text 2 is quiet and individual. Arjun is an "independent contractor" who rides alone, and "Everything is worth it... until you add it up" sounds like tired arithmetic, not defiance. It's also worth noticing that Text 1's dignity belongs only to "men", while Text 2 finds its one moment of grace in a woman at a gate.

Together the texts suggest that work and wages aren't enough without the third thing the 1931 speaker named, respect, and in both eras respect depends on being seen as a person rather than counted as a figure.

sets.title: Visiting Hours
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original short scene from a play. Dana and Michael are adult siblings waiting while their father is in surgery. They have not spoken for eleven years. A header is a grain harvester.
sets.body:
A family room in a regional hospital, late at night. A vending machine hums. Two vinyl chairs with an empty one between them, a box of tissues, a television mounted high on the wall with the sound off. DANA, forty, in work clothes, sits very upright with her handbag on her knees. MICHAEL, thirty-six, in a football jumper, enters with two cups of machine coffee. He holds one out. She looks at it.

MICHAEL: White, no sugar. (Beat.) Or has that changed too?

DANA: It's fine. (She takes it. She does not drink.)

MICHAEL: (sitting, leaving one chair between them) Nurse said another hour. Maybe two.

DANA: I spoke to the surgeon.

MICHAEL: Course you did.

DANA: Someone had to.

(Pause. On the television, silent, a man points at a weather map.)

MICHAEL: He asked for you. Before they took him down. He said, 'Is Dana coming?'

DANA: (a fraction too fast) And what did you say?

MICHAEL: I said you were on your way.

DANA: I was.

MICHAEL: Eleven years is a long way.

(DANA puts the coffee down on the floor, carefully, as if it might go off.)

DANA: You don't get to do that. You were here. You got to be here.

MICHAEL: Got to.

DANA: Yes, got to. You got the farm, and the ute, and the Sunday roasts, and him telling everyone at the pub how you'd turned the place around —

MICHAEL: I got the overdraft. I got him falling off the header in August because he wouldn't let me drive it. I got him calling me by your name when the sugar was low.

(Silence. DANA looks at him for the first time.)

DANA: My name?

MICHAEL: Dana, get the gate. Dana, where's the — (He stops.) Three, four times a week. Like you'd just gone into town.

(DANA picks up the coffee again. She holds it with both hands.)

DANA: He never rang.

MICHAEL: Neither did you.

DANA: I wrote. At Christmas. I wrote every Christmas.

MICHAEL: I know. They're in the dresser. (Beat.) He opened them. He just didn't know what you wanted him to say.

DANA: Sorry. I wanted him to say sorry.

MICHAEL: (quietly) Yeah. Well. He's not a sorry kind of bloke. He's more of a get-the-gate kind of bloke.

(Something that is almost a laugh escapes DANA. She covers her mouth. MICHAEL moves, slowly, into the empty chair between them. Neither speaks. On the television, the weather map shows rain moving in from the west.)

DANA: That'll be good for the crop.

MICHAEL: Yeah. It will.

(The lights fade slowly as they watch the silent screen.)

Dana uses it to make staying sound like a privilege: "You were here. You got to be here." Michael throws it back as a flat fragment, "Got to.", questioning her assumption, and her insistence, "Yes, got to", leads into a list of what she imagines he gained: "the farm, and the ute, and the Sunday roasts". His last item, "I got him calling me by your name", turns the scene. What Dana thought she was shut out of was itself haunted by her absence.

questions.model:
The scene presents reconciliation not as a resolution but as a change in where the siblings look and where they sit. It moves from guarded hostility, through a revelation that changes Dana's understanding of the past, to a shared silence in which the conflict is put on hold rather than settled.

The opening sets up the conflict through clipped, barbed dialogue. Michael's "Or has that changed too?" turns an offer of coffee into an accusation. Dana's competence is met with his sarcastic "Course you did.", and her reply, "Someone had to.", implies he isn't up to it. The muted television, where "a man points at a weather map", underlines how badly they are communicating.

The turning point is a revelation. When Michael says their father called him "by your name when the sugar was low", the argument stops, and "DANA looks at him for the first time" marks her shift from defensiveness to attention. His broken-off imitation, "Dana, get the gate. Dana, where's the", shows that the father's love came out in the language of everyday farm work. Dana's "Sorry. I wanted him to say sorry." is the most exposed moment in the scene, and Michael's dry answer, that their father is "not a sorry kind of bloke", turns grief into a joke they can share. "Something that is almost a laugh escapes DANA" captures how tentative the connection still is.

Then the staging does what the dialogue can't. Michael "moves, slowly, into the empty chair between them", closing the gap from the opening, and "Neither speaks". Silence, which was a weapon earlier, has become something they can share.

The ending is deliberately understated. "That'll be good for the crop." is the first thing Dana says in the language of the farm, and of their father, and Michael's "Yeah. It will." accepts it. The rain "moving in from the west" offers hope, but it's still only on a silent screen, and the father's surgery is unresolved. The reconciliation is real but fragile: a beginning, not an ending.

sets.title: Review: The Counting Season
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original book review of a fictional novel. The novel, its author and the reviewer are invented. The Newell Highway is an inland road in New South Wales.
sets.body:
There is a kind of novel that announces itself as important in its first sentence and then spends three hundred pages trying to live up to the announcement. Lena Marchetti's debut is not that kind of novel. The Counting Season begins with a girl counting the cars that pass her family's service station on the Newell Highway, and for a long time it seems content to keep counting. This is its great strength and, eventually, its problem.

The girl is Bianca, fourteen, and the year is 1998. Her father has stopped speaking, not out of anger, the novel is careful to tell us, but because 'the words had worn out, the way a tyre wears out, from the inside where you can't see it'. Bianca's mother runs the station, the till, the roadhouse kitchen and the family's silence with the same tired efficiency. Nothing much happens. A truck driver leaves a book behind. A cousin visits from Griffith. A dog goes missing and comes back.

Marchetti's prose is remarkable for what it refuses to do. It refuses to explain. It refuses, almost entirely, to describe the father's illness in clinical terms; instead we see it the way Bianca sees it, through objects: his reading glasses folded on the windowsill for a whole season, the newspaper still in its plastic sleeve. These chapters have the patience of a long drive, and like a long drive they produce in the reader a strange, receptive calm in which the smallest event, a magpie on a bowser, becomes luminous.

The trouble arrives in the final forty pages, when the novel seems to lose its nerve. Having trusted silence for so long, Marchetti suddenly gives the father a lengthy speech at a family dinner in which he explains himself, his war, his marriage and his regrets, in complete and grammatical paragraphs. It is beautifully written. It is also, I think, a mistake. After three hundred pages teaching us to read what is not said, we are handed everything, and the effect is less like revelation than like the radio coming on too loud in a quiet car.

Still, it would be churlish to let an ending outweigh a book this assured. Marchetti has a gift for the overlooked: for the inland, the in-between, the people who serve you petrol and do not expect to be remembered. The Counting Season is a debut of real distinction, flawed in the way that ambitious first novels often are, by not quite trusting its own best instincts.

Read it slowly. Then argue with the ending.

Four stars.

sets.title: Ghazal for the City I Am Leaving
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original ghazal, a form from Arabic, Persian and Urdu poetry made of self-contained couplets. In this version every couplet ends with the same word, and in the final couplet the poet addresses herself by name, as ghazal poets traditionally do. The poet, Ayesha, is fictional. Auburn, Granville, Harris Park and Blacktown are suburbs of western Sydney.
sets.body:
I have packed the kettle and the good knives. It takes a year to leave.
The jacarandas will flower without me. They have never learned to leave.

At Circular Quay the ferries shoulder in and out like patient cattle.
Only the wake behind them, widening, rehearses how to leave.

My mother crossed two oceans with one suitcase and a tin of seeds.
She grew curry leaves in Blacktown. She said you never wholly leave.

Each room goes back to being a room once the pictures are down.
The nail holes stare like questions I forgot to ask. And still I leave.

My friends say, You'll be back, the way you wish a swimmer luck
at the edge of the surf: half blessing, half permission to leave.

My grandfather kept the key to a house across a border he never crossed again.
I have the key now. It opens nothing. It is how we learned to leave.

This city never asked me to belong. It simply let me stay.
That is the kindness of large cities: they make it easy to leave.

From the plane I will try to name the suburbs by their lights,
Auburn, Granville, Harris Park, and lose them one by one, and leave.

Ayesha, when they ask you over there where you are from,
say the name of a city that taught you how to leave.

Because each couplet in a ghazal stands on its own, the refrain is what holds them together, so the repetition makes a whole out of fragments. That suits a speaker trying to hold her scattered memories together as she goes.

questions.model: Leaving is presented as an inheritance passed down the generations, and each generation carries an object that stands in for what can't be carried. The mother "crossed two oceans with one suitcase and a tin of seeds". The seeds stand for a culture transplanted rather than abandoned, and the specific suburban result, "She grew curry leaves in Blacktown", shows that heritage taking root somewhere new. Her saying, "you never wholly leave", is one family lesson: where you come from stays with you. The grandfather's key teaches a darker one. He kept it for "a house across a border he never crossed again", an image of displacement and loss, and the speaker's flat short sentences, "I have the key now. It opens nothing.", hand down a grief that has no practical use but can't be thrown away. The couplet ends "It is how we learned to leave", as if leaving has become a family skill, almost a tradition. Setting her own departure among these generations, the speaker continues the pattern, with one difference: unlike her grandfather, she leaves by choice.

questions.model:
The poem suggests that a place doesn't simply grant belonging, and leaving doesn't simply end it. Belonging is made through attention, memory and inheritance, and it is often understood most fully at the moment you go.

The poem begins by separating being allowed to stay from belonging. "This city never asked me to belong. It simply let me stay." That is ambivalent. The city's indifference is "the kindness of large cities", because it demands nothing, but the same quality makes it "easy to leave". Tolerance, the poem implies, isn't the same as belonging.

The family couplets show that people, not places, make belonging. The mother turns Blacktown into home by growing "curry leaves" from her "tin of seeds", so belonging is cultivated, literally rooted, through care. Her claim that "you never wholly leave" suggests places also live on in the people who leave them, and the grandfather's key, which "opens nothing" but is still kept, supports this. Belonging can outlast the place it belongs to.

Leaving also sharpens the speaker's attachment. She names ordinary things: "the kettle and the good knives", the "nail holes" that stare "like questions I forgot to ask", and the run of suburbs, "Auburn, Granville, Harris Park". Her love shows itself in exact naming. Yet losing the suburbs "one by one" from the plane window suggests this belonging is fragile and depends on memory.

The final couplet pulls this together. Addressing herself as "Ayesha", the speaker imagines being asked where she's from and tells herself to "say the name of a city that taught you how to leave." That paradox is the poem's central insight. Sydney's gift isn't permanence; it's the ability to carry a place inside who you are. Belonging, then, is portable and inherited, like the seeds and the key: never wholly left, and never wholly kept.

sets.title: At Merrin Bay, 1891
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an original poem written in the style of the 1890s. Text 2 is an original contemporary poem. Both describe the same fictional Sydney beach, Merrin Bay. An ocean pool is a swimming pool built into the rocks at the edge of the sea.
sets.body:
Behold the breakers, how they rise and fall
In ordered ranks along the crescent sand,
As if some mighty Hand had drilled them all
To come and kneel, and kiss the patient land.

Here, safe behind the railings, ladies stroll
With parasols against the morning glare,
And gentlemen in flannels, on the whole,
Approve the ocean, and the ocean air.

But I have seen, when evening empties out
The promenade, and lamps are lit in town,
The sea come in without a word of doubt
And wash the careful footprints of us down.

So let us build our railings as we must,
And post our rules, and set the bathing hour;
The sea, that keeps no reckoning of our dust,
Was here before, and will outlast our power.

pair.title: Merrin Bay, Six A.M.
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
The ocean pool is already full of old men
doing slow laps in their caps, like thoughts
returning to the same idea.
A woman in a hijab and leggings
jogs the length of the promenade
with her earbuds in, mouthing a song.
Two backpackers asleep on the grass
under a single towel. A council truck
raking last night off the sand:
cans, a thong, somebody's birthday balloon
still trying to leave.

Nobody here owns the water.
We just turn up, the way it does,
twice a day, without being asked,
and stand in it to our knees, gasping,
and say, every morning, as if we'd just invented it,
it's freezing, it's beautiful, it's freezing.

Behind us the old pavilion
has been a gym, a nightclub, a restaurant,
and is now, the sign says, Coming Soon.
The waves don't read it.
They keep arriving
in their long, untidy lines,
not kneeling to anyone.

The opening list gathers all sorts of people with no hierarchy: "old men / doing slow laps", "A woman in a hijab and leggings", "Two backpackers asleep on the grass". The flat, list-like syntax gives each of them equal weight, and swimmers moving "like thoughts / returning to the same idea" make repetition feel comforting. questions.model:
Both poems recognise that the sea doesn't care about human attempts to order it, but they respond differently. Text 1 moves from colonial confidence to a solemn sense of mortality; Text 2 starts from humility and finds in the same indifference a source of shared, everyday joy. Read together, they trace a shift from controlling nature to living alongside it.

Text 1 opens by imposing order on the sea. Its regular quatrains and alternating rhyme match the breakers' "ordered ranks", which kneel "and kiss the patient land" as if drilled by "some mighty Hand". The capital H suggests a providential order where nature serves people. Text 2 rejects that picture. Its waves keep coming "in their long, untidy lines, / not kneeling to anyone." The echo makes Text 2 sound like a reply, swapping hierarchy for freedom.

The people on the shore are different too. In Text 1 the beach is about decorum: ladies stroll "safe behind the railings" and gentlemen "Approve the ocean", a gently ironic line that shows how presumptuous it is to pass judgement on the sea. In Text 2 the railings are gone. The old men, the jogger and the sleeping backpackers share the space equally, and "Nobody here owns the water."

Both poems end by admitting the sea's power. Text 1 concedes that people will "post our rules, and set the bathing hour", but the sea "keeps no reckoning of our dust" and "will outlast our power"; "dust" brings in death. Text 2 makes the same point more lightly: whatever the pavilion turns into next doesn't matter, because "The waves don't read it."

Form reinforces the difference. Text 1's elevated diction, starting with "Behold", tries to master its subject, while Text 2's free verse and conversational voice, ending in the gasped "it's freezing, it's beautiful, it's freezing", act out a looser relationship where people take part rather than preside. Both poems suggest the sea humbles every era. What changes is whether that humility feels like dread or delight.

sets.title: The Keeper's Daughter
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an extract from an original short story written in the style of the late nineteenth century. Cape Morrow is a fictional headland on the New South Wales coast. A ketch is a small sailing vessel; the gallery is the walkway around the top of a lighthouse.
sets.body:
My father kept the light at Cape Morrow for eleven years, and in all that time I do not believe he slept a night through. The lamp was his child more than I was; he rose to it at every hour, trimmed its wick, wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, and wrote in the log in a hand so small and regular that it seemed less like writing than like the stitching of a hem.

We were three miles from the nearest neighbour and forty from the nearest town, and our only visitors were the supply ketch, which came when the sea allowed, and the wind, which came whether it was allowed or not. I was twelve when my mother died, and from that time it was I who cooked, and mended, and read aloud to my father in the evenings from the only three books we owned, while the light went round above us and laid its long white arm across the water, again and again, like a man feeling in the dark for something he has dropped.

It was in the winter of 1883 that he began to speak of the other light.

He said it first at supper, quite plainly, as one might mention a change in the weather. There was a light to the south, he said, beyond the reef, where there was no light and never had been. He had seen it from the gallery at two in the morning: a small, steady yellow, low on the water, not moving with the swell as a ship's lamp would.

I said, as a daughter should, that it was surely a fishing boat, or a reflection, or the moon on wet rock. He agreed that it must be. He wrote nothing of it in the log.

But after that he went up to the gallery more often, and stayed longer, and when I brought him his tea at midnight I would find him not tending the lamp at all, but standing at the south rail with the telescope, quite still, as if the cold had stopped him. Once I looked where he was looking. I saw nothing but the dark, and the reef breaking white, and our own beam passing over the water and away.

'There,' he said. 'Do you see it? It answers ours.'

I said that I did not. He lowered the glass and looked at me for a long moment, with an expression I have never forgotten, which was not anger, nor fear, but a kind of pity, as though it were I who could not see what was before me.

In the spring the inspector came with the ketch and found the log in perfect order. My father was transferred to a light in a more settled district, near a town with a church and a school, and I was sent to the school, and in time I married, and the years did what years do.

I have never told anyone that before we left Cape Morrow, on our last night, I climbed to the gallery alone. I do not know what I hoped for. The sea was black and the reef was white, and our light went round, and round, and for a moment, low on the water to the south, I thought I saw a small yellow light, steady as a candle in a window, waiting for someone to come home.

I did not mention it to my father. He would only have pitied me.

questions.model: Cape Morrow's isolation creates an atmosphere of loneliness and unease, in which the father's strange vision seems both believable and disturbing. The family lives "three miles from the nearest neighbour and forty from the nearest town", and the exact distances stress how cut off they are. Their only visitors are the ketch and "the wind, which came whether it was allowed or not", personified as an intruder. The lighthouse routine adds a sense of confinement: the father tends the lamp "at every hour", and the daughter reads "from the only three books we owned". At night the sea is all stark contrast, "the dark, and the reef breaking white", a gothic palette of black and white. Most of all, the beam is like "a man feeling in the dark for something he has dropped", a simile that fills the setting with searching and loss. In a world this remote, repetitive and nocturnal, the other light seems like something solitude would naturally produce, and that's exactly what makes it unsettling.

questions.model:
Light in this extract moves from duty to desire. The lighthouse beam stands for the father's disciplined service and his isolation, while the mysterious "other light" holds a longing his solitary life can't satisfy. The ending, when the daughter glimpses it too, changes the father from a man who may be losing his mind into one who saw something true about loneliness.

At first, light means duty and confinement. The lamp is "his child more than I was", which shows his work pushing his family aside, and his log, written like "the stitching of a hem", suggests order and self-control. Yet the beam itself lays "its long white arm across the water, again and again, like a man feeling in the dark for something he has dropped". Already it suggests searching and loss, as if it carries the grief for his wife that he never speaks.

The other light brings in longing. It appears "where there was no light and never had been", "a small, steady yellow", warmer than the lighthouse's white. Its steadiness contrasts with the beam's restless turning, hinting at a stillness the father lacks. When he says "It answers ours", he seems to read it as a reply to his lonely signalling, a companion in the dark. The daughter offers rational explanations "as a daughter should", and "He wrote nothing of it in the log", which marks the vision as private, outside the order of duty.

The ending reshapes all of this. Years later the narrator confesses that on the last night she too saw a light "steady as a candle in a window, waiting for someone to come home." The simile makes the light domestic, an image of home and return, perhaps of the mother and the family life the lighthouse pushed aside. The father's look of "pity" now seems justified rather than mad, and the final line, "He would only have pitied me", reverses their positions. Isolation, the motif suggests, doesn't produce delusion so much as a clearer view of what you long for.

sets.title: Seen
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original short story that includes transcribed group-chat messages. The characters are fictional Year 11 students. Bracketed words such as [screenshot] describe images in the chat.
sets.body:
The group chat is called Year 11 Survivors, and it has six members, and for most of the year it has been the loudest room I am ever in.

Tonight it is quiet. I check it in the bathroom, under the desk, at the dinner table under the edge of the plate, which Mum has said she will confiscate my phone for, and which she has not done yet.

Here is what it looked like at 4.12 pm:

YEAR 11 SURVIVORS
Priya: guys
Priya: did anyone else see what Jade posted
Mia: ??
Priya: [screenshot]
Mia: oh
Ellie: oh no
Priya: like I'm not saying anything
Priya: I'm just saying
Mia: she literally said she was sick
Ellie: lol
Seen by Jade, Tom

Jade is the sixth member. The screenshot was of Jade, at the beach, on the day of Priya's birthday lunch, which Jade had said she couldn't come to because of a migraine. In the photo she is laughing at something outside the frame. She looks, I think, happier than I have seen her all year, which is a strange thing to notice about a photo you're supposed to be angry about.

Seen by Jade.

Nobody has typed anything since. The little words sit there at the bottom of the screen like a cough in an exam room. I have started a message four times.

Me: hey jade are you
(deleted)
Me: guys maybe we should
(deleted)

At school Jade sits with us the next day as if nothing has happened, and nothing has, out loud. Priya offers her a chip. Mia talks about the chemistry test. Ellie laughs at a joke a little too hard and a little too late. Jade eats the chip. Under the table, I can feel all our phones in our pockets like small warm stones.

That night Jade leaves the chat. The app tells us, in the same neutral grey it uses for everything: Jade left the group.

Mia: well
Priya: honestly her choice
Ellie: [heart reaction]
Tom: has anyone done the chem worksheet

I put my phone face down on the desk. Then I turn it over again. Then I open a new message, just to Jade, and for a long time I look at the empty box, and the cursor blinking in it like something breathing.

I type: hey. the beach looked nice.

I look at it for a long time. Then I add: I'm glad you went.

I press send before I can stop myself, and the message goes, and sits there, Delivered, and then, after a minute that takes about an hour,

Seen.

And then the three dots. Appearing, disappearing, appearing again, like someone deciding whether to come out of the water.

questions.model:
The text suggests that group chats intensify both the closeness and the cruelty of friendship, because they turn private feelings into public performances. It also suggests that real connection is still possible through small, individual acts of courage.

At first the chat is intensely social, "the loudest room I am ever in". Calling it a room makes the online space feel physical, and the narrator checks it compulsively, even "under the edge of the plate". Friendship here never stops, and it's always performed.

That performance makes a quiet cruelty possible. The screenshot turns Jade's private day into public evidence, and "Seen by Jade" means the person being judged watches the judging. At school the conflict carries on offline, unspoken: "nothing has, out loud." Phones sit in pockets "like small warm stones", which suggests the chat is carried into face-to-face life as a weight, even a weapon.

The app's neutrality makes it harsher still. "Jade left the group" appears "in the same neutral grey it uses for everything", as though the technology flattens the end of a friendship into routine information, and the group goes back to chemistry homework.

Against all this, the narrator turns from the group to one person. Her private message, "hey. the beach looked nice.", then "I'm glad you went", swaps judgement for acceptance. The three dots appear "like someone deciding whether to come out of the water", linking back to the beach and leaving the outcome open. Group chats, the text suggests, can turn friendship into surveillance, but the same tools can carry a sincere, one-to-one act of care.

sets.title: I Have Optimised My Life, and I Would Like It Back
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original satirical opinion column. The columnist, her neighbour and the products mentioned are fictional.
sets.body:
At 5.15 every morning, my ring vibrates. It is a smart ring, which means it is smarter than I am, a fact it reminds me of daily. It has measured my sleep and found it wanting. 'Your readiness score is 61,' it tells me, in the tone a vet uses about an elderly dog. 'Consider a gentle day.'

I do not have a gentle day. Nobody who wears a smart ring has ever had a gentle day. Instead I drink 500 millilitres of water with a pinch of Himalayan salt, because a man with very white teeth on the internet told me to, and I stand in front of a lamp that is supposed to imitate the sunrise, which is happening, for free, outside my window.

Then I journal. My journal has prompts. Today's prompt was: What are three things you are grateful for? I wrote: the journal, the lamp, the salt. I believe this is what experts call engagement.

By 7 am I have meditated (eleven minutes, guided by an app with a voice like warm honey that occasionally asks me to upgrade to Premium), taken my supplements (nine, in a pill organiser with more compartments than my kitchen), and logged my mood on a scale of one to five. I always choose four. I am afraid of what happens if I choose three.

I want to be fair. Some of this works. I sleep a little better. I drink more water. I am, by most measurable standards, a more optimised person than I was three years ago. It is just that I am no longer sure who I optimised me for.

Because the strange thing about wellness, as it is currently sold, is that it is never finished. There is no moment at which the ring says: You are well now. Go outside. Talk to someone. Eat a sandwich without photographing it. There is only the next metric, the next supplement, the next eleven-minute programme to fix the anxiety caused by the previous eleven-minute programme.

My grandmother, who lived to ninety-four, did not know what her heart-rate variability was. She knew what time the bowls club opened and which of her neighbours needed soup. She walked to the shops because the shops were where people were. If she had owned a smart ring, I suspect she would have used it to stir her tea.

I am not going to throw the ring away. I paid too much for it, which is itself a symptom. But this morning, when it told me my readiness score was 58, I did something radical. I said, out loud, to a piece of jewellery: 'That's nice, love.' And then I went next door and asked Mrs Okonkwo if she wanted to come for a walk.

She did. We talked about her tomatoes. I have no idea what it did for my metrics.

It was, by any measure, the best part of my day.

The column presents the wellness industry as a business that manufactures the anxieties it claims to cure, and it uses irony, bathos and exaggeration to show how absurd that is.

Irony exposes the industry's habit of selling what used to be free. The columnist stands in front of a lamp "supposed to imitate the sunrise, which is happening, for free, outside my window". The interruption "for free" punctures the product's value and makes buying it look ridiculous.

Bathos deflates the language of self-improvement. Her answer to the journal's gratitude prompt is "the journal, the lamp, the salt", and her deadpan "this is what experts call engagement" mocks the industry's jargon. The meditation app has "a voice like warm honey" but asks her "to upgrade to Premium", so even calm has a price tag.

Exaggeration shows that the buying never ends: a pill organiser "with more compartments than my kitchen", and "the next eleven-minute programme to fix the anxiety caused by the previous eleven-minute programme". The repetition makes the cycle sound circular and self-feeding, which is the satire's main charge.

The ring sharpens the point. It speaks "in the tone a vet uses about an elderly dog", a simile that makes the technology condescending, and it will never say "You are well now. Go outside." Those imagined commands show what the product can't offer, because a customer who feels well stops paying. The column exposes wellness as an industry whose business model depends on customers never quite feeling well enough.

The column balances satire and sincerity very effectively. Its humour doesn't just mock wellness culture; it clears the ground for a more serious definition of wellbeing as connection and attention. It works mainly because she satirises herself as much as the industry, which makes her sincere conclusion believable rather than preachy.

The first half is mostly satire. The ring speaks "in the tone a vet uses about an elderly dog", and the gratitude list reads "the journal, the lamp, the salt"; exaggeration and irony like this expose how absurd measured, purchased wellness is. If the column stopped there, it would just be entertaining.

The turn comes with a deliberate change of tone: "I want to be fair. Some of this works." The short, plain sentences and the concession signal that she means it, and she sounds reasonable rather than cynical. When she admits, "I am no longer sure who I optimised me for", the joke becomes a real question about whose interests self-optimisation serves.

She then offers another model through her grandmother, who knew "which of her neighbours needed soup" and walked to the shops "because the shops were where people were". The anecdote could slide into nostalgia, but humour keeps it from going soft: she would have used a smart ring "to stir her tea".

The ending acts the message out instead of stating it. Telling the ring "That's nice, love" and asking Mrs Okonkwo along for a walk show wellbeing as connection. "We talked about her tomatoes. I have no idea what it did for my metrics." puts the unmeasurable above the measurable, and the last line, "It was, by any measure, the best part of my day", turns the language of metrics against itself.

You could argue that a walk with a neighbour is a personal answer to a structural problem. But within a personal column, the mix of self-mockery and sincerity makes the point persuasively, and it sticks.

sets.title: Driving Lessons
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original memoir extract. The narrator and her mother are fictional. Penrith is in western Sydney; the M4 motorway leads towards the Blue Mountains.
sets.body:
My mother taught me to drive the year my father left, in a white Corolla with a cracked dashboard and a cassette player that held one tape. The tape was a compilation my father had made years before, labelled DRIVING in his square capitals, and neither of us took it out.

The first lesson was in the car park of the shopping centre at Penrith on a Sunday evening, after the shops had closed. My mother sat in the passenger seat with her handbag on her lap, clutching it the way you would hold a cat at the vet. She said, 'Mirror. Signal. Look over your shoulder. Your actual shoulder, Rach, not just your eyes.' She said it before I had even started the engine.

I stalled eleven times. I know because she counted, out loud, in a voice that went higher with each number, until at eleven she put her hand over her face and made a sound I didn't recognise. I thought she was crying. She was laughing. She laughed until she had to wipe her eyes with the sleeve of her work cardigan, and then she said, 'Again,' and I did it again, and the car didn't stall, and we rolled very slowly past the trolley bay at about four kilometres an hour, both of us silent, as if we'd crossed a border.

That was in March. All through that year we drove on Sunday evenings: the car park, then the back streets, then the M4 at dusk with the trucks shouldering past. My mother was not a natural teacher. She stamped on an imaginary brake in the passenger footwell. She gripped the door handle on roundabouts. She said 'Gently' so often that it became a kind of weather. But she never missed a Sunday, even when she had worked a double shift at the hospital, even the week the house went on the market.

We did not talk about my father. We talked about blind spots and following distances and whether the man in the Commodore had seen us. I understood, even then, that the car was the one place in our lives where the rules were clear, and that she was teaching me them with a kind of fierceness, as if they might stand in for the other rules, the ones that had stopped working.

My last lesson was the day before my test. I drove us up to the mountains without being asked, the long climb past Glenbrook, and at a lookout near Wentworth Falls I pulled over and turned the engine off. The valley below was full of blue haze, the way it always is in the photographs, and for once it was not a disappointment.

My mother looked at it for a long time. Then she reached over and pressed eject on the cassette player, and the tape came out with a small mechanical sigh, and she put it in her handbag.

'You can choose the music now,' she said.

I passed my test the next day. On the drive home I drove and she sat beside me, and for the first time all year, her hands were in her lap.

The narrator explains that "the car was the one place in our lives where the rules were clear", and that her mother taught them "with a kind of fierceness, as if they might stand in for the other rules, the ones that had stopped working". "the other rules" suggests the unspoken expectations of marriage and family that broke when the father left. Their conversations shift the same way: "We did not talk about my father. We talked about blind spots and following distances". Putting the two side by side shows that talking technique lets them spend time together and look after each other without facing grief head-on, and "blind spots" quietly hints at what they avoid looking at. From the very first lesson the mother insists on precision, "Your actual shoulder, Rach, not just your eyes", determined to prepare her daughter for a world that has already proved unreliable. The rules turn into a language of love and protection.

questions.model:
In the first lesson the mother is anxious, controlling and fragile, holding herself together by giving instructions; in the final lesson she is calm and trusting, ready to let go. The change runs from protection to release, and it suggests her recovery is tied up with her daughter's independence.

In the first lesson her anxiety shows in physical detail. She grips her handbag "the way you would hold a cat at the vet", and fires off "Mirror. Signal. Look over your shoulder." before the engine is even on; the clipped commands show how badly she needs control. She counts the stalls "in a voice that went higher with each number", building to a release the narrator misreads: "I thought she was crying. She was laughing." The confusion suggests her feelings are very close to the surface.

Through the year the anxiety carries on in comic gestures. She "stamped on an imaginary brake" and said "Gently" so often "that it became a kind of weather". Yet she never missed a Sunday, "even the week the house went on the market", and that reliability shows the determination underneath the nerves.

By the final lesson she is quiet and still. The narrator drives "without being asked", and her mother "looked at it for a long time", a thoughtful pause that couldn't be further from the earlier stream of orders. Then she ejects the father's tape, which comes out "with a small mechanical sigh". It marks the end of an era, and the personified sigh carries both relief and sadness. "You can choose the music now" hands authority to her daughter and perhaps frees her from the past as well.

The last image completes the comparison: "for the first time all year, her hands were in her lap." The hands that clutched the handbag are finally at rest. Teaching her daughter to drive has also been the mother's way of steering through grief, and the two of them arrive at a new beginning together.

sets.title: Letter from France, 1917
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an original letter written in the style of the First World War, from a fictional Australian soldier, Harry, to his mother. Text 2 is an original memoir extract by Harry's fictional great-niece, a century later. Nell is Harry's younger sister.
sets.body:
France, 2nd October 1917

Dear Mother,

Your parcel came on Tuesday and I want you to know that the socks were the best thing that has happened to me since August, and that I am wearing both pairs at once, which the sergeant says is against regulations, though he has not said which regulation. The cake did not survive the journey as a cake, but we ate it as crumbs with a spoon and it was very fine crumbs.

We are out of the line for a few days, in a village I am not allowed to name, sleeping in a barn with a great many other fellows and a great many rats, who are the only ones of us that look well fed. There is an old woman here who sells us eggs and calls us all Australie, as if it were one person's name, and I suppose to her it is.

You are not to worry. I know that you will, so I am telling you not to so that you will at least worry less. I am well and I keep my head down, as Father told me, and Jack Pearce from the dairy is in my section, and we talk about home until the others tell us to shut up.

I think about the creek at the bottom paddock a good deal. When I get back I am going to sit on the bank there for a whole day and not do one useful thing, and you are not to call me in for tea.

There are things here I will not write about, and you are not to ask me about them when I come home. I will tell you instead about the eggs, and the old woman, and how the poplars along the road go yellow all at once, like a lamp turned up.

Give my love to Father and to Nell, and tell Nell she can have my bike until I want it back.

Your loving son,
Harry

pair.title: The Biscuit Tin
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
The letter lives in a biscuit tin in my grandmother's wardrobe, between her wedding certificate and a lock of hair in an envelope that just says Harry, which I was not allowed to open as a child and have still not opened.

My grandmother was Nell. She was nine when her brother wrote to their mother about the socks and the cake and the yellow poplars, and she was ninety-one when she showed me the letter for the first time, her hands so careful with the paper that it seemed she was holding something that might wake.

'He never came back for the bike,' she said.

That was all she said about it. I knew, the way you know family facts without ever being told them, that Harry had been killed in France a few weeks after the letter was written, and that his mother had never sat by the creek again either. I knew there was a photograph in the hallway of a young man in a slouch hat whose face I had walked past ten thousand times without looking at.

What I did not know, until I read the letter myself, was that he was funny. That he made jokes about socks and regulations. That he told his mother not to worry so that she would worry less, which is the kind of logic I recognise, because my grandmother used it on me my whole life.

I have read the letter perhaps fifty times now. The line I return to is the one where he says there are things he will not write about. I used to read it as protection, a son sparing his mother. Lately I read it differently. I think he was protecting the letter, too: keeping one small piece of paper free of the war, so that something he made would stay about eggs and poplars and a creek.

If that was his plan, it worked. A hundred years later, it is the eggs I remember.

My grandmother died last spring. The bike went long before that, of course, sold or rusted or given away. But I have the tin now, and the letter, and the envelope I have still not opened, and I have decided that I am not going to. Some things you keep by not looking.

questions.model:
Read together, the texts suggest that war is remembered as much through what is held back as through what is said. Harry's deliberate silences protect his family and the ordinary texture of his life, and the memoir shows a later generation honouring him by respecting those silences rather than filling them in.

In Text 1 Harry chooses what to keep. He fills the letter with small domestic details: the cake eaten "as crumbs with a spoon", the old woman who calls the soldiers Australie "as if it were one person's name", the poplars turning yellow "like a lamp turned up". The rest he refuses outright: "There are things here I will not write about, and you are not to ask me about them". The violence of the war stays unspoken.

Text 2 shows both what that choice cost and how well it worked. Harry's death is never narrated. It is only a family fact, and Nell's single sentence, "He never came back for the bike", turns a casual promise into an elegy. The memoir copies Harry's restraint, putting grief into an object instead of a statement.

The narrator then rethinks the silence. She used to read it as "protection", but comes to see Harry as "protecting the letter, too", keeping it "free of the war". "A hundred years later, it is the eggs I remember" confirms that his selective record shapes how he survives: as a funny, observant young man, not a casualty.

In both texts, holding back becomes an act of love. Harry tells his mother not to ask; the narrator decides not to open the envelope marked "Harry", because "Some things you keep by not looking." Her choice answers his across a century.

So the texts suggest that war is remembered most humanely not through complete testimony but through fragments chosen with care, and that silence, far from wiping out the past, can be what keeps it whole.

sets.title: What You Cannot See
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original speech by a fictional hydrologist (a scientist who studies water). She is addressing a community meeting in Tellum Creek, a fictional inland town. All figures in the speech are part of the fiction. An aquifer is a layer of rock that holds groundwater.
sets.body:
Thank you for coming out on a cold night. I know some of you have driven forty minutes to be here, and I know some of you have heard people like me talk about water before, and gone home no wiser and a good deal crankier. I'll try to do better.

I want to start with a glass of water. This one. It came out of the tap in this hall twenty minutes ago. It's clear, it's cold, it tastes fine. And it is about eleven thousand years old.

That's not a figure of speech. The water under this town sits in sandstone, in tiny spaces between the grains, the way water sits in a sponge. Most of it fell as rain a very long time ago and has been seeping down, slowly, ever since. Every time you turn on a tap in Tellum Creek, you are drinking the weather of a world with no wheat, no fences, and a very different coastline.

Here's the problem. We are taking it out faster than it is going in. Not by a little. Our measurements from the monitoring bores show the level dropping by about forty centimetres a year. You can't see that. Nobody wakes up and notices that an aquifer is forty centimetres lower. There is no flood, no fire, no photograph for the front page. That is exactly what makes it dangerous.

Now, I'm not here to tell you who to blame. The farms use it. The town uses it. The new feedlot will use it. Most of you are some combination of all three, and some of you are related to all three. Blame is easy, and it doesn't put a single litre back in the ground.

What I am here to tell you is that the decision in front of the council next month is not really about this year, or the next five. It's about whether there is water under Tellum Creek for the kids at the back of this room when they are as old as I am. And the trouble with groundwater is that by the time you can see the problem, it's too late to fix it in a lifetime. Eleven thousand years to fill. A few generations to empty.

So I'm asking you for something unusual. I'm asking you to care about something you will never see. I'm asking you to be the kind of town that thinks in centuries, like the water does.

You don't have to take my word for it. The monitoring data is public. I'll put the link on the screen, and I'll stay as long as anyone wants to ask me questions, including the cranky ones.

And before you go, have a glass of water. Taste it properly. It's the oldest thing in this room, older than the hall, older than the town, older than the river. It got here before us. The question is whether it will still be here after we're gone.

The speaker makes an invisible problem urgent by turning it into concrete pictures, treating its very quietness as the danger, and framing the decision in terms of time and children.

She starts by making the hidden aquifer something you can imagine. Water sits in sandstone "the way water sits in a sponge", a familiar picture of something nobody in the room will ever see. And "you are drinking the weather of a world with no wheat, no fences" links a daily habit to deep time, so the water starts to feel precious.

Then she turns invisibility itself into the threat. Having given the decline, "about forty centimetres a year", she lists what is missing: "There is no flood, no fire, no photograph for the front page." The three absent disasters set groundwater loss against the crises that usually get attention, and "That is exactly what makes it dangerous" spells out the argument in one short sentence.

sets.title: Grade One at Forty-Three
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original personal essay. The writer, her daughter and her violin teacher are fictional. Ashfield is a suburb of Sydney; music students sit graded practical exams, beginning at Grade One.
sets.body:
At forty-three, I sat my Grade One violin exam in a church hall in Ashfield, between a seven-year-old in a tartan pinafore and a nine-year-old who was, I later learned, sitting Grade Three. I was the only candidate whose mother had not driven them there. I was also the only one who cried in the car park afterwards, though in fairness to me, I had passed.

I started lessons the year my daughter left home. I told people it was to keep my brain young, which is the kind of reason adults are allowed to give for doing something useless. The truth is that I had wanted to play the violin since I was eight, when a woman played at my grandfather's funeral and I understood, for the first time, that a sound could be sad on someone's behalf. My parents said violins were expensive and I would give up. They were right on both counts, eventually. But it took me thirty-five years to give up, and then another five to start again.

Nobody warns you how bad you will be. Not slightly bad, not endearingly bad, but bad in a way that makes the dog leave the room. For the first six months, every note I played sounded like a door being opened slowly in a horror film. My teacher, a patient woman of about twenty-five, would listen with her head on one side, as if trying to hear the music I intended behind the music I made, and then say, kindly, 'Okay. Let's try that again.'

What I had forgotten, in thirty years of being competent at things, was what it feels like to be a beginner. Adults arrange their lives to avoid it. We do the jobs we're good at, cook the meals we know, take the routes we've driven a thousand times. We call this experience, and it is, but it is also a kind of fortress, and after a while you forget you are living inside one.

Being a beginner at forty-three meant being bad in public, or at least in front of my teacher and the dog. It meant practising scales while my neighbours could hear. It meant accepting that I would never be good, not really, not in the time I have left, and doing it anyway. That last part is the hardest, and the most important. Almost everything we are taught about effort assumes a reward at the end of it: the job, the grade, the trophy. The violin offers no such bargain. I will never play in an orchestra. Nobody will ever pay to hear me. I practise because, for twenty minutes a day, I am fully absorbed in trying to make one sound slightly less terrible than the last, and that absorption is its own reward.

I sometimes think about the woman at my grandfather's funeral. I don't know her name. She was probably an amateur too, someone's neighbour, asked to play because she could. She was not, I suspect, very good. It didn't matter. She played, and an eight-year-old in the second row heard grief turned into something you could hold.

My exam piece was a folk tune, sixteen bars long. I played it slightly too fast and missed the F sharp in bar eleven. The examiner wrote: Good sense of line. Enjoy your playing.

I am trying to.

questions.model:
I find her argument that accepting you'll never be good is "the hardest, and the most important" part of being an adult beginner largely persuasive. She earns it through frank personal experience. It does, however, depend partly on having time and money, which she doesn't fully acknowledge.

Her honesty is her best asset. She refuses to romanticise learning: she is "bad in a way that makes the dog leave the room", and her early notes sound like "a door being opened slowly in a horror film". Because she admits failure so vividly, her claims about its value sound believable rather than sentimental.

The core of her argument is a clear contrast. "Almost everything we are taught about effort assumes a reward at the end of it", but "The violin offers no such bargain." The plain sentences "I will never play in an orchestra. Nobody will ever pay to hear me." make her giving up on achievement concrete, and being "fully absorbed" for "twenty minutes a day" sounds like an appealing, achievable alternative.

The funeral memory adds emotional weight. If an unremarkable amateur could make a child hear "grief turned into something you could hold", then excellence can't be the measure of what music is worth.

The argument only reaches so far, though. Lessons, instruments and spare time cost money, as her parents' objection that "violins were expensive" hints, and for many adults the obstacle isn't pride but circumstance. Still, as a personal essay it persuades. She shows the value of trying instead of just telling us, and her final line, "I am trying to.", has exactly the humility she recommends.

sets.title: For Sale: 14 Wattle Crescent
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an original real-estate advertisement. Text 2 is an extract from an original short story about the same house. The suburb, agency, agent and characters are fictional. STCA means subject to council approval.
sets.body:
FOR SALE | 14 Wattle Crescent, Ironbark Hill
Auction Saturday 10 am, on site

Family Haven with Room to Grow

Lovingly held by the same family for over thirty years, this solid brick home is ready for its next chapter. Set on a generous 650 square metre block in one of Ironbark Hill's most tightly held pockets, it offers an exciting opportunity to renovate, extend or rebuild (STCA).

Inside, a light-filled living area flows to a classic kitchen brimming with potential. Three bedrooms, all with built-ins, and a family bathroom offer plenty of space for growing families, while the sunroom, currently used as a sewing room, would make a perfect home office.

Outside, a sun-drenched backyard with established fruit trees and a much-loved cubby house provides endless scope for the kids, or for the landscaper of your dreams. A single lock-up garage with internal access completes the picture.

Walk to schools, shops and transport. Opportunities like this are rare. Inspect today and imagine the possibilities.

Contact: Sharon, Ridgeline Realty
Disclaimer: All information has been obtained from sources believed to be reliable, but its accuracy cannot be guaranteed. Interested parties should rely on their own inquiries.

pair.title: The Last Night at Wattle Crescent
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
On the last night my mother wanted fish and chips, eaten off the paper on the kitchen floor, because the table had already gone to my brother's.

'Like when we moved in,' she said. 'We didn't have a table then either.'

The house echoed now. Without the rugs and the bookcases, every sound we made came back to us slightly changed, the way your own voice sounds on a recording. My mother kept touching things as she passed them: the light switch with the chip in its corner, the doorframe in the hall with our heights pencilled up it in three colours, the window latch she'd been asking my father to fix since 1994.

'The agent said the kitchen was brimming with potential,' she said. 'I said, I know, it's been brimming for thirty years.'

After we ate, she wanted to go out to the yard. It was nearly dark. The lemon tree was heavy with fruit no one would pick, and the cubby house my father built the summer I turned six leaned slightly to the left, the way it always had, because he'd measured once and cut twice. My mother stood beside it with her hand on the roof as if it were the head of an old dog.

'They'll knock it down,' she said. 'The people who buy it. They'll knock the whole lot down and build one of those houses with a cinema in it.'

'You don't know that.'

'I read the ad,' she said. 'Room to grow. Imagine the possibilities.' She said the words carefully, as though translating them. 'That means a bulldozer.'

I didn't argue. She was probably right. Ironbark Hill had become the kind of suburb where the old brick houses came down one by one and the new ones went up to the edges of the blocks, white and square, with no trees.

We stood there while the yard went dark around us. Somewhere down the street a dog barked and another one answered. My mother picked a lemon, and then another, and put them in the pockets of her cardigan.

'For the new place,' she said. The new place was a unit on the second floor with a balcony the size of a bath mat.

'You'll need a tree for those,' I said.

'I'll need a lot of things.' She looked at the house, at the sewing room window, at the dark kitchen where we had eaten off the floor. 'I'll make do.'

At the gate she stopped and looked back, not for long, and then she put her arm through mine, and her pockets full of lemons knocked gently against my hip all the way to the car.

questions.model: The objects show that what the mother is attached to is the lived history of the house, and the objects hold that history. Walking through the empty rooms she keeps "touching things", and the details, "the light switch with the chip in its corner, the doorframe in the hall with our heights pencilled up it in three colours", turn ordinary fittings into a record of family life. The pencilled heights literally measure time. The window latch she had been "asking my father to fix since 1994" is funny and tenderly exasperated, and it quietly reminds us the father isn't there. In the garden, the cubby leans "because he'd measured once and cut twice", which captures his imperfect work and his love together. Her hand rests on its roof "as if it were the head of an old dog", a simile full of affection for something old and loyal. Finally she pockets lemons "For the new place", carrying part of the old life with her, and they knock "gently against my hip". The past will come along, small but persistent.

questions.model:
The two texts look at the same house from opposite directions. The ad presents a property defined by what it could become; the story presents a home defined by what it has been. Each shows something the other hides, and together they expose the gap between market value and lived meaning.

The ad speaks the language of opportunity. Its headline, "Family Haven with Room to Grow", and its closing command, "Inspect today and imagine the possibilities", invite buyers to picture their own lives there. History only appears as a selling point. The home has been "Lovingly held by the same family for over thirty years" and is "ready for its next chapter", phrases that squash three decades into a cliché and move on.

Text 2 lingers on exactly what the ad skips. The pencilled heights, the chipped light switch and the cubby that leans "because he'd measured once and cut twice" are what those thirty years were made of. The ad sells the cubby as "much-loved" scope "for the kids, or for the landscaper of your dreams"; the story shows a woman resting her hand on its roof "as if it were the head of an old dog".

The story also sees through the ad's euphemisms. The mother's dry joke that the kitchen has "been brimming for thirty years" deflates the agent's phrase, and she translates "Room to grow. Imagine the possibilities." into what it really means: "That means a bulldozer."

But Text 1 isn't simply lying. Its disclaimer that the information "cannot be guaranteed" is honest about what kind of text it is, and buyers do need to imagine their own lives somewhere. Text 2 is partial too. Its nostalgia sees mostly loss, while the mother herself concedes, "I'll make do."

Together the texts suggest a house is two things at once: an asset valued for what it could become, and a home valued for what it has been. The story's attention to objects reveals exactly what the ad's language is designed to leave out.

sets.title: Saltwater Hymn: A Five-Star Review
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 and Text 2 are original reviews of the same fictional play by two different fictional reviewers. The play, playwright, actors and theatre are invented.
sets.body:
Saltwater Hymn | Harbourside Theatre | Five stars

Every few years a play arrives that makes you want to stop strangers in the foyer and tell them what they have just seen. Saltwater Hymn is that play.

Dani Reyes's debut follows three generations of women in a fishing family on the south coast, over a single night when a boat fails to return. That is all the plot there is, and it is all the plot the play needs. For ninety unbroken minutes, Reyes lets her characters talk, argue, sing and wait, and the waiting becomes almost unbearable, in the best sense.

The performances are extraordinary. As the grandmother, Lorraine Fitch delivers a monologue about her husband's first boat that had the audience so silent you could hear the hum of the lighting rig. Kiara Dunn, as the youngest daughter, is all fury and wit until the final scene, when a single line, spoken almost under her breath, undoes everything she has built.

The design deserves its own review. A sloping floor of grey boards suggests both a jetty and a deck; a strip of blue light along the back wall rises and falls like a tide all night, so slowly that you notice it only when it has gone.

Yes, there are moments when the dialogue strains for poetry. Who cares? This is a play unafraid of feeling, and it trusts its audience to feel with it. I left in tears, and I was not alone.

Go. Take someone you love. Then call your mother.

pair.title: Saltwater Hymn: A Two-and-a-Half-Star Review
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
Saltwater Hymn | Harbourside Theatre | Two and a half stars

There is a great deal to admire in Saltwater Hymn, and a great deal to endure.

Dani Reyes clearly has an ear for the rhythms of coastal speech, and in its first half-hour the play crackles: the three women circle each other with the wary humour of people who have shared a kitchen too long. Lorraine Fitch, as the grandmother, is magnificent, and her monologue about her husband's first boat is the best writing in the play.

The trouble is that it is also the longest, and it is followed by several more. As the night wears on, the characters stop talking to each other and start making speeches, each one more lyrical than the last, until the effect is less like a family in crisis than like a poetry reading in a power blackout. When the youngest daughter finally speaks the line that is meant to break our hearts, it arrives so heavily signposted that I had guessed it twenty minutes earlier.

The design is handsome, if a touch obvious: the strip of blue light along the back wall, rising and falling like a tide, is lovely for ten minutes and a metaphor for the next eighty. And ninety minutes without an interval is a long time to hold one note, however beautiful.

None of this means Reyes lacks talent. She plainly has it, in abundance. What she needs now is the confidence to trust silence as much as she trusts language, and an editor brave enough to cut her favourite lines.

The audience around me wept. I admired the craft and checked my watch.

questions.model: This reviewer's criticism is funny rather than cruel, and that makes the negative verdict more persuasive. The opening, "a great deal to admire... and a great deal to endure", announces a balanced review with a comic sting in "endure". The central simile, that the play becomes "less like a family in crisis than like a poetry reading in a power blackout", blows the problem of over-lyrical speeches up into an image you remember. Praise gets turned against the play too: the best monologue is "also the longest". The tide of light is "lovely for ten minutes and a metaphor for the next eighty", a neat contrast implying the symbolism is obvious. The last sentence, "I admired the craft and checked my watch.", is bathos. High praise sits next to an everyday gesture, and the whole verdict is summed up in one deflating action. The humour makes the reviewer seem sharp and fair, so we trust the criticism.

questions.model:
The two reviews describe the same production and reach opposite verdicts, which suggests a review tells you a lot about its reviewer's values. But both record the same features, and each concedes the other's case, so their differences reveal the reviewers alongside the play, not instead of it.

They share evidence and weigh it differently. Both praise the grandmother's monologue, but where Text 1 offers the audience's silence as proof of extraordinary acting, Text 2 adds that "the best writing in the play" is "also the longest". Both see the strip of blue light rising and falling "like a tide". Text 1 admires a subtlety noticed "only when it has gone"; Text 2 finds it "lovely for ten minutes and a metaphor for the next eighty". Even the running time is "ninety unbroken minutes" to one and "a long time to hold one note" to the other.

The climactic line shows their values most clearly. In Text 1 it is spoken "almost under her breath" and "undoes everything she has built"; in Text 2 it "arrives so heavily signposted" that the critic saw it coming. One values being emotionally swept away, the other values surprise and restraint, and their closing lines seal the contrast: "I left in tears, and I was not alone" against the bathos of "I admired the craft and checked my watch."

Still, the play limits both judgements. Text 1 admits "the dialogue strains for poetry", and Text 2 acknowledges that "The audience around me wept." Both critics saw the same strengths and the same flaws; they disagree about which matter more.

So the differences do reveal the reviewers' priorities, but not at the play's expense. Read together, the reviews give a fuller picture than either one alone: a moving, overwritten debut whose worth depends on whether you want to be swept away or surprised.
